v: But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.
The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!”
He called for lights, sprang in, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas,
brought them out, and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
They spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house.
He took them the same hour of the night and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household.
He brought them up into his house, and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly, with all his household, having believed in God.
b: In the last devotion, for the freedom of a slave girl, Paul and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into the inner prison with their feet in the stocks. The passage stopped in the darkest cell of the prison.

Today we continue with that night. In a few short hours Luke records a song, an earthquake, a sword, a question, and a meal. Look closely: the greatest miracle was not the earthquake but that no one fled after it; the greatest release was not the loosening of the chains but that a man holding a sword was saved.
I. “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God”—A Song While the Wounds Still Bled
Verse 25: “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.”

The wounds on their backs were still oozing blood, their feet were spread in the stocks, and they sat against the damp wall unable to sleep. At midnight what they did was not groan, not complain, not discuss what to do tomorrow. They prayed, and then they sang. “Listening” is a very attentive word—the prisoners did not overhear in passing; they pricked up their ears. A prison has every kind of sound, except that no one had heard singing.

Happiness is like a thermometer, rising and falling with the environment; joy is like a thermostat, set from within. Paul’s environment had dropped to the lowest—falsely accused, humiliated, beaten, locked up—the thermometer had long since burst. But the thermostat inside him was not broken, because it was set by the Holy Spirit, not by the environment. Years later, writing from another prison to the Philippians, he said, “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4), a sentence he first sang in the inner prison at Philippi.

To give thanks in everything does not mean everything is good but that in everything there is the good Lord. One who follows the Holy Spirit with the heart can sing at midnight; one who leans on himself with the head is still calculating in the daytime.
• Someone is listening: how I respond in affliction, there are always people nearby with ears pricked.
II. “Suddenly there was a great earthquake… everyone’s chains were loosened”—God’s Answer Beyond What Was Asked
Verse 26: “Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. Immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains were loosened.”

This earthquake came with perfect timing: just as they were singing, the foundations shook, the doors all opened, and everyone’s chains—not only Paul’s—were loosened. Paul did not ask for an earthquake; he only prayed and praised, and God answered in a way far beyond all he asked or thought.

But Luke immediately wants us to see something stranger: the doors were open and the chains loosed, yet no one ran away. A group of prisoners, in a prison with its doors open, and not one moved. That song had held them. They had seen something more attractive than freedom, in those two who were singing.
• God’s answer exceeds what is asked: what I pray is a small matter, and He often moves the whole foundation.
• Something more attractive than freedom: is there something in me that makes people not want to leave when they see it?
III. “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!”—The Freedom of Not Running

Verses 27 and 28: “The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, ‘Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!’”
By Roman rule, if a prisoner escaped, the guard paid with his own life (12:19). The jailer knew what awaited him—better to end it himself than to be tried and executed. He drew his sword.

At that very moment Paul’s voice came out of the darkness: Don’t harm yourself! We are all here. The door of the inner prison stood open, the stocks were loose, and Paul was free—yet he did not leave. He stayed for the man who had locked him in the stocks.

This is the freedom of self-denial. A person of self, on gaining freedom, first uses it for himself; a person emptied of self, on gaining freedom, first looks to see whether there is a man beside him holding a sword. When the door opened, what Paul saw was not an exit but a man about to die.
• On whom is my freedom used: the freedom, gifts, and opportunities God gives me—the first one I think of is myself or the person beside me?
• The one who stays: willing to stay for someone who once hurt me, and not run away.
IV. “What must I do to be saved?”—“Believe in the Lord Jesus”
Verses 29 to 32: the jailer called for lights, sprang in, and fell down trembling before Paul and Silas, then brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”

A few hours earlier he had locked these two men in the inner prison; now he fell at their feet. “Sirs” in the original is “lords”—a guard calling prisoners lords. From that song, that earthquake, that “Don’t harm yourself,” he had sensed that in these two was a greater answer.

Paul’s answer was a single sentence: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” Not “you must first make it up to us,” not “you must first do this and that.” “Do” was the jailer’s word, and “believe” was Paul’s. Salvation is not by doing but by believing. And “you and your household” does not mean that one person’s faith automatically saves a household, but that the promise extends to the household; so in verse 32 they “spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house,” and every person had to hear it himself and believe it himself.
The core of the gospel is this simple—simple enough for a jailer shaken in the middle of the night to understand at once, and simple enough for anyone today to respond at once.
• Ask the right question: am I asking “what must I do to keep what is mine,” or “what must I do to be saved”?
• A household hears: the promise of salvation extends to my household, but each person must hear and believe for himself.
V. “Washed their stripes… were baptized”—Two Washings and a Meal

Verses 33 and 34: “He took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his. He brought them up into his house, and set a table before them, and rejoiced greatly, with all his household, having believed in God.”

Luke writes of two washings. First the jailer washed Paul’s stripes—wounds he had locked up himself and paid no heed to; then the jailer was baptized—his sins washed clean by the Lord. A person first washing another’s wounds and then being washed by the Lord is a beautiful order. “The same hour of the night,” “immediately”—Luke stresses it repeatedly: he did not wait for daylight or for safety; having believed, he was baptized.

Then he brought them up into his own house and set a table. A few hours earlier it was the house of a man about to kill himself; now this house had a table, two guests with cloth on their backs, and a household that “rejoiced greatly.” “Rejoiced greatly” is the word for exultation, a joy that leaps.

Philippi now had a second household. The first was Lydia’s, the second the jailer’s—a wealthy woman and a rough soldier, who in a lifetime would never have sat at the same table; now they were one church. God’s system is not a group of similar people but a group of people who let Jesus be King.
• Wash others’ wounds first: the first act of one who is saved is to look back at whom he has hurt.
• A household’s joy: does my household have this leaping joy that comes from believing in God?
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Door Opened and They Did Not Run—Freedom for the Sake of Others
That night, two men’s doors were opened. Paul’s prison door opened, and the jailer’s heart opened. The one whose prison door opened did not flee, so the one whose heart opened was saved.

Self-denial is not nothingness but entering the limitless. Paul sang at midnight not because he was numb but because within him was a source not set by circumstances; he did not leave when the door opened not because he was foolish but because his freedom was not for himself. The freedom of the person of self ends when it is used on himself; the freedom of the person emptied of self, used on others, gives birth to a church.

And at the center of it all is that one sentence, “Believe in the Lord Jesus.” Paul did not leave the jailer’s attention on himself—not on his song, his endurance, or the nobility of his not running—he pointed the man to the Lord at once. What letting Jesus have all the glory looks like in a prison is just this: everything I do is only so that people ask, “What must I do to be saved?” and then I hand them to the Lord.
a: Praise at Midnight
Joy is set from within, not set by the environment.
God’s Answer Beyond What Is Asked
I pray about a small matter, and He moves the whole foundation.
When the Door Opens, Look at the One Beside Me
Use freedom, gifts, and opportunities first on the man holding the sword.
One Sentence Pointing to the Lord
Hand people to the Lord Jesus; do not leave them on me.
Wash Others’ Wounds First
The first act of salvation is to look back at whom I have hurt.
q: Do you have an “inner prison” now—the darkest situation, the one you least want to be in? Could you open your mouth to sing a song there? If you cannot, what is holding you back?

Paul did not flee when the door opened, because he saw a man with a sword. Is there a door in your life that has opened—an opportunity to get away—yet the Lord wants you to stay first for someone? Who is that person?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that in the inner prison at Philippi You heard the song at midnight; You answered a hymn with an earthquake and saved a man with a sword by a single “Don’t harm yourself.” The freedom of not running when the door opens is greater than the freedom of running out.
Lord, we confess that our joy is often a thermometer, rising and falling with circumstances; place within us that thermostat set by You, so that even in the darkest cell we can sing. Remove from us the self that, on gaining freedom, uses it first for itself, and teach us, when the door opens, to see first the man beside us holding the sword. Let our mouths be simple, saying only “Believe in the Lord Jesus,” pointing people to You and not leaving them on ourselves. May our homes be like the jailer’s home, with a table, guests, and a leaping joy because we have believed in You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, “Let those men go.”
The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go; now therefore come out and go in peace.”

But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!”
The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans,
and they came and begged them. When they had brought them out, they asked them to depart from the city.
They went out of the prison, and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them, then departed.
b: In the last devotion, the midnight song, the earthquake, and the jailer with his sword ended at a dinner table: the jailer and his whole household rejoiced greatly because they had believed in God.

Day broke. The magistrates sent word to release them quietly. The story could have ended easily—out of prison, out of the city, and on their way. But Paul said a sentence that startled everyone: “We are Romans.” In this devotion we see how one emptied of self uses his rights, and what he did last before leaving a city.
I. “Let those men go”—The Magistrates Wanted to Settle It Quietly

Verses 35 and 36: “But when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, ‘Let those men go.’ The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, ‘The magistrates have sent to let you go. Now therefore come out, and go in peace.’”

“Sergeants” in the original are “rod-bearers,” the very men who beat Paul with rods the day before. Why did the magistrates release them so early? Perhaps the night’s earthquake had frightened them, or perhaps they felt the lesson was enough and driving them out of the city would end it. Their calculation was to send these two Jews away without a sound, and yesterday’s matter would be over.

The jailer said “go in peace”—he meant it. This man who locked them up yesterday and washed their wounds today was eager for his new brothers to get out of danger quickly. His kindness was not wrong, but he did not yet understand: some things cannot simply pass in peace.
• The temptation to settle privately: over an injustice, the person of self fights to the end, the timid wants it over quickly; what does the Lord want me to do?
II. “We are Romans”—Why Did Paul Speak Only Now?

Verse 37: “But Paul said to them, ‘They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison. Do they now release us secretly? No, indeed, but let them come themselves and bring us out.’”

Roman law forbade beating a Roman citizen without trial, much less with rods. Paul was a Roman citizen by birth (22:28), and Silas evidently was too. Every step the magistrates took yesterday—no trial, stripping, beating, prison—was a serious offense, and in severe cases would cost them their office.

Why did Paul not say so yesterday? Perhaps in the uproar no one heard; perhaps he chose not to, for if he escaped by his citizenship, what would become of the believers in Philippi who did not have that status? He would rather first suffer as they did.

Then why did he say it today? Not for himself—yesterday’s beating had already been received, and speaking today could not take it back. He spoke today for those who would remain in the city. If he slipped away quietly, the Philippians would remember that those two preachers were criminals beaten and driven out, and those who believed them were of the same sort. If the magistrates themselves came to bring them out, the whole city would know: these two were innocent, and the church they left behind was not an unlawful assembly.

Rights are like an umbrella. The person of self opens it to cover himself; the person emptied of self holds it over his brothers. Paul did not open it yesterday because opening it would shelter only himself; today he opened it because opening it could shelter a whole church.
• On whom do I use my rights: the status, resources, and relationships in my hands—the last time I used them, was it for myself or for my brothers?
• Suffer first, then speak: only one willing to suffer with his brothers first speaks words that carry weight.
III. “Let them come themselves and bring us out”—Justice, Not Revenge

Verse 37 (latter half) to verse 39: “‘Let them come themselves and bring us out.’ The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans, and they came and begged them. When they had brought them out, they asked them to depart from the city.”

Notice what Paul wanted. He could have accused the magistrates and demanded compensation; he asked for neither. He asked for one thing: you come yourselves and bring us out publicly. Yesterday’s humiliation was public, so today’s clearing must be public too. What he wanted was justice, not revenge.

“Begged” in the original carries the sense of “pleaded” and “appealed”—the magistrates who yesterday ordered the beating came today to plead humbly. It was a great reversal, but Paul took no enjoyment in it. He did not say, “See how you treated me yesterday,” and did not make the magistrates feel one bit more embarrassed. He sought justice, and then let go.

This is what humility looks like before rights: not giving up justice, but not taking one’s own share from it. Pride seizes the chance when wronged to lift itself up; humility seeks justice for those who are owed it and does not take extra for itself.
• Seek justice, not revenge: over an injustice, ask for clearing, but do not take one bit more for myself.
• Don’t enjoy the reversal: when the other bows his head, do I loosen my grip, or press down once more?
IV. “Asked them to depart from the city”—Submitting to the Boundary of Authority
Verse 39: the magistrates “asked them to depart from the city.” This “asked” is polite, but the meaning is clear: please go.

Paul went. He had just proved himself right and the other side guilty, yet once the magistrates spoke he submitted. He did not say, “I am a Roman citizen and I will stay as long as I like.” What he contended for was not the right to stay in the city but the innocence of the gospel in the city; the innocence won, he left.

There is a very fine line here: when to say “No, indeed,” and when to say “Good, I’ll go.” Paul did both, only a few verses apart. The key to discerning is not principle but focus: if the focus is on self, both will go wrong—contending where one shouldn’t, staying where one should go; if the focus is on Jesus and His church, one knows which sentence to speak.
• Say no when it is time to say no, and go when it is time to go: discernment depends not on principle but on whose is the focus.
V. “They entered into Lydia’s house, and when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them”—Before Leaving, See the People
Verse 40: “They went out of the prison and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.”

After leaving prison, Paul did not first look for a place to nurse his wounds, and did not leave the city at once; he went to Lydia’s house. There were already “brothers” there—Lydia’s household, the jailer’s household, perhaps also the girl who had been set free. A few days earlier this city had not one believer; now it had a church.

“Encouraged” is the same word as the “encouragement” with which the Jerusalem letter comforted everyone in chapter 15. With the wounds on his back not yet healed, he first went to encourage others. Before leaving, he put the people on his heart. Notice also that “we” disappears here—Luke stayed in Philippi (appearing again only at 20:5), and Paul left his closest co-worker to accompany this newborn church.

Years later, writing from prison to this church, Paul said, “because of your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now” (Philippians 1:5). “The first day” was this day. Philippians, called the epistle of joy, was written to a church born out of prison.
• See people before leaving: before leaving a place, is the last thing I do to encourage people, or to settle affairs?
• Leave the best: Paul left Luke in Philippi. Am I willing to leave my best for others?
The Light of the 321 Principles: Open Your Rights for Others, and See People Before Leaving

Philippi was a Roman colony, a group of Roman citizens living on Macedonian soil, loyal to a distant emperor. The church Paul left here was a colony of heaven—“For our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20)—a people who let Jesus be King, living in Caesar’s city. This is building God’s system: not overthrowing the city but forming within it a domain belonging to another King.

And the way Paul used his Roman citizenship is exactly how those in this system should be. He had the right; yesterday he did not use it, today he did; when he used it, it was not to win something back for himself but to open an umbrella for his brothers; once opened, he let go, and when they said go, he went. Self-denial is not having no rights but rights no longer used for oneself: for the person of self, a right is a weapon; for the person emptied of self, a right is an umbrella.

Last of all he went to Lydia’s house. People matter more than tasks—justice was recovered and the magistrates bowed, but what his heart was set on last was those few new believers. This chapter began with a young man, Timothy, and ended with a small church; in between were closed doors, open doors, beating, and an earthquake, but from beginning to end what Paul looked at was people. One who lets Jesus be King looks this way.
a: Don’t Let It Pass Quietly
If something unjust should be cleared for the sake of the brothers, clear it.
Hold Rights Over Others
With status, resources, and relationships, first think of whom they can shelter.
Seek Justice, Not Revenge
Ask for clearing, but take not one bit extra for myself.
Go When It Is Time to Go
When innocence is won, submit, and do not contend for the right to stay.
See People Before Leaving
On leaving any place, the last thing is to encourage the brothers.
q: Paul did not use his citizenship yesterday but did today; when he used it, it was not for himself but for his brothers. What right, status, or resource do you hold? The last time you used it, was it to cover yourself or to hold over others?

After leaving prison, Paul first went to Lydia’s house to encourage the brothers before leaving the city. Think of the last time you left a post, a group, or a relationship—was the last thing you did settling affairs, or encouraging people?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that what Your servant left in Philippi was not a victory but a church. Thank You for letting us see that Paul first suffered with his brothers and then held his rights over them; he sought justice yet took not one bit extra; when the magistrates asked, he submitted and left. In Caesar’s city You established Your heavenly colony.
Lord, we confess that the rights in our hands are mostly used to cover ourselves; when wronged we want revenge, at a reversal we want to enjoy it, and when it is time to go we will not go. Remove from us the self that treats rights as a weapon, and teach us to treat them as an umbrella held over our brothers. Give us Paul’s discernment, to know when to say “No, indeed” and when to say “Good, I’ll go”; and make the last thing we do, wherever we leave, to go and see people. May the city where we live have a domain belonging to You through a people who let You be King, and may all the glory be Yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
Paul, as was his custom, went in to them, and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”
Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and not a few of the chief women.
But the unpersuaded Jews took along some wicked men from the marketplace, and gathering a crowd, set the city in an uproar. Assaulting the house of Jason, they sought to bring them out to the people.
When they didn’t find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers  before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also,
whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!”
The multitude and the rulers of the city were troubled when they heard these things.
When they had taken security from Jason and the rest, they let them go.
b: In the last devotion, the magistrates of Philippi sent sergeants to release them quietly, but Paul would not go quietly: we are Romans, you beat us publicly, and now you release us secretly? The magistrates, afraid, came themselves to ask them to leave the city. The two came out of prison, first went to Lydia’s house to encourage the brothers, and only then left.
The welts on their backs had not yet healed when they were on the road again. In these nine verses are the birth of a church, a riot, and an accusation that was accidentally yet perfectly accurate.
I. “Passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica”—Wounds Not Yet Healed, Already on the Road

The three place names in verse 1 are really the name of one road: the Via Egnatia, the highway the Romans built to move troops, running across Macedonia. From Philippi to Thessalonica it is about a hundred miles, roughly three days’ walk. Luke writes it plainly, but we must not forget: the two men walking this road had just days before been stripped, beaten with many rods, and had their feet put in the stocks.

Thessalonica was the capital of the province of Macedonia, a free city with a busy port. There was a Jewish synagogue here—the previous two cities evidently had none, so Paul did not linger in them; he was looking for those who read the Old Testament, so that the gospel could be told from Scripture. The Romans built this road so that legions could march fast; they did not know that one day it would carry the news of a crucified King into the heart of the empire.
• Wounds are not a reason to stop: the Lord’s servant does not wait until everything is well to move; he goes forward while it still hurts.
• God borrows the world’s roads: the industry, city, or platform where you are may be the very highway God has prepared for the gospel.
II. “As his custom was” and “from the Scriptures”—He Had a Constant Way

Verses 2 and 3: Paul went in “as his custom was,” and “for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead.”

“Reasoned” in the original is “conversed,” not quarreling but explaining through question and answer. “Explaining” in the original is “opening,” the same word as when the Lord “opened their minds” on the road to Emmaus; “demonstrating” is “setting before,” like setting out dishes on a table one at a time.

Paul’s content had three steps: the Christ “had to” suffer—this was the hardest hurdle for Jews, who awaited a triumphant Messiah, not a crucified one; the Christ had to rise; and only then, this Jesus is that Christ. The first two steps were told from the Old Testament, and only in the third was Jesus put in. This is what “Scripture is my standard” looks like in preaching: he did not rely on the exorcism in Philippi, nor on the prison doors flung open; he relied on Scripture. Experiences get questioned and miracles get explained away; when Scripture is opened, people must face what God Himself has said.
• Have a constant way: people with a steady spiritual life have practices that do not shift with mood—regular reading, gathering, and prayer.
• Open the Bible first: when talking faith with people, am I speaking of my feelings, or first setting before them what God has said?
III. “Some of them were persuaded”—A Church Is Born

Verse 4 names three groups: Jews in the synagogue, “some”; “devout Greeks,” God-fearing Gentiles who attended the synagogue without being circumcised, “a great multitude”; and “not a few of the chief women,” women of standing in the city. Few Jews and many Gentiles—1 Thessalonians confirms that this church was mainly Gentile believers, who had “turned to God from idols” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

In roughly a month a church was born. Paul later wrote, “our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 1:5). The word was Paul’s; the power was the Holy Spirit’s; a person can set forth the message, but only the Holy Spirit can make people “persuaded.”
• The fruit is not in my hands: I am responsible for speaking clearly, and the Holy Spirit is responsible for making people believe.
• A church is born: when a group of people are persuaded and join the Lord, they naturally become a church.
IV. “Jealous” and “another king, one Jesus”—The Accusers Spoke the Most Accurate Truth

Verses 5 to 7: the riot began with “jealousy.” It was not a doctrinal dispute but the sight of devout Gentiles and chief women in the synagogue following Paul in batches. Jealousy is the most honest expression of the self—I do not care what the truth is; I care whether the ones who follow are following me. “Wicked men of the marketplace” in the original are “idlers in the marketplace,” who would stir up trouble for a little reward.

They stormed into Jason’s house, and not finding them, dragged Jason before the “politarchs.” This title was almost never found in Greek literature, and some doubted that Luke had it right; later, inscriptions unearthed in Thessalonica carved exactly this word.

The content of the accusation is the most intriguing: “These who have turned the world upside down”—a group of men with welts on their backs were said to have upset the whole empire; “saying that there is another king, one Jesus”—this was the political crime of treason. But think carefully: not one of these two statements was wrong. The gospel really does turn the world upside down; Paul really did preach a King, whose name is Jesus.

The problem is the word “another.” A nation cannot have two emperors, and a heart cannot have two thrones. If you say Jesus is my King, you are saying I am not. This is the whole meaning of letting Jesus be King: not adding another chair beside my existing throne, but my standing up from that one chair and letting Him sit.
• Recognize the face of jealousy: when I see others followed and used by God and feel uncomfortable, at that moment admit it is the self speaking.
• What standing up from the chair looks like: when making a decision today, first ask “what does He want me to do,” not “what do I want.”
V. “When they had taken security… they let them go”—A Bond That Closed a Door

Verses 8 and 9: the politarchs’ alarm was justified. The free city’s privileges were granted by Rome, and if rumors of “treason” reached Rome, the whole city would be implicated. They handled it shrewdly: neither condemning nor letting it go, they took “security”—making Jason guarantee with his property that these two would not appear in the city again.

The effect was that Paul could not go back to Thessalonica, or Jason would lose everything. This is probably what Paul later meant by, “we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, once and again—but Satan hindered us” (1 Thessalonians 2:18). A legal document became the enemy’s instrument of obstruction.

But though the door closed, God’s work did not stop. Paul could not go back, so he sent Timothy; Timothy brought back good news, and Paul wrote a letter—1 Thessalonians, very likely the earliest-written book of the New Testament. A door closed, and a book of Scripture was written because of it, comforting countless people for two thousand years.
• Satan’s hindrance is real: there is no need to call every setback God’s kind intention; some things are simply the enemy hindering.
• But God has more roads: the door closed on you today may be just the time God wants you to write a “letter.”
The Light of the 321 Principles: Another King
The accusation at Thessalonica is the most accurate one-sentence summary of the gospel in the whole book of Acts: “saying that there is another king, one Jesus.”

We often treat letting Jesus be King as a spiritual slogan, but the people of Thessalonica heard its true weight—this is something that alarms magistrates and costs Jason everything he owns. For there can be only one King. What a life of self does best is to hold two kings in the heart at once: on Sunday Jesus is King, on Monday I am King; when things go well Jesus is King, when I am offended I am King. In Scripture there is no such dual service. Those unbelieving Jews were jealous precisely because their own throne was threatened; and Jason, with his own house and property, stood bond for that “other king.”

Change begins with me. Today the question is not “is the world willing to let Jesus be King,” but “am I?” When one person is willing, that person’s home, workplace, and relationships become His domain—and God’s system begins there.
a: Move Forward with Wounds
Don’t wait until everything is well; follow the Lord’s road while it still hurts.
Keep a Constant Way
Make reading, prayer, and gathering habits that do not shift with mood.
Recognize the Face of Jealousy
When I see others followed and used and feel uncomfortable, admit it is the self speaking.
Stand Up from the Chair
Before deciding, ask “what does He want me to do,” not “what do I want.”
Don’t Stop Work When a Door Closes
When hindered, ask the Lord to show another road; it may be the time to write a “letter.”
q: “Saying that there is another king, one Jesus”—if someone accused you of this, would your life offer enough evidence for the charge to stand? In which area is the evidence least?
Is there a door you plainly see yet cannot enter? Besides praying for it to open, are you willing to ask the Lord whether He wants you to do something else outside the door?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Paul and Silas walked the Roman highway with welts on their backs, and in Thessalonica You brought a church to birth. The road men built for themselves, You used to carry the gospel; the bond men set to obstruct, You used to bring about a letter that comforts multitudes.
Lord Jesus, those who accused Your servants said, “another king, one Jesus.” We confess that this is true, and ask You to make it true in us. Forgive us for keeping two chairs in our hearts, letting You be King when things go well and sitting back down ourselves when offended. Remove from us the self that is jealous when it sees others followed, and give us the heart of Jason, willing to stand bond with all we have for You, the King. Be King in each of our decisions, so that we first ask what You want us to do, and then see what we want. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Many of them therefore believed; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men.
But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Beroea also, they came there likewise, agitating the multitudes.
Then the brothers immediately sent out Paul to go as far as to the sea, and Silas and Timothy still stayed there.
But those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that they should come to him very quickly, they departed.
b: In the last devotion, the magistrates of Thessalonica took Jason’s bond before releasing them. That bond amounted to a curfew: if Paul and Silas appeared in the city again, Jason would lose everything. So they could neither stay nor turn back.

So it was another night, another quiet departure. But this time the place they reached became the most enviable audience in the whole book of Acts—people who heard the message and neither believed at once nor opposed at once, but went home and opened their Bibles.
I. “Immediately sent them away by night”—Brothers Who Saw Them Off in the Night
Verse 10: “The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea.”

“Immediately” shows urgency; “by night” shows danger. Several times in his life Paul escaped by night: the wall of Damascus, the harbor of Jerusalem, and now Thessalonica. Those who sent them off were brothers who had believed for only a month. The church was newly born and the pastor was already leaving; yet these people did not complain. What they did was protect, see off, and commit the man into the Lord’s hand.

Beroea was about fifty miles southwest of Thessalonica, off the Roman highway, a relatively remote mountain town. The Roman statesman Cicero once called it a “town off the beaten track.” Paul chose it probably precisely because it was not on the main road—pursuers would not easily think of it. But on arrival, “when they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue.” The city could change, the way could not; on arrival, still the synagogue first.
• Seeing off is ministry: protecting God’s servant and standing firm when he leaves is the first ministry of a newborn church.
• Remote is not withdrawal: in a place off the highway, Paul did exactly what he did in the capital.
II. “More noble” and “with all eagerness”—Nobility Is an Open Heart
Verse 11 (first half): “Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all eagerness.”

“More noble” in the original means “better born,” and later came to mean broad-minded and not narrow. Luke does not say the Bereans were smarter or more learned; he says their hearts were more “noble.” The Jews in Thessalonica, hearing Paul, first felt jealousy; the people of Beroea, hearing the same message, first “received the word with all eagerness”—in the original, “with complete readiness.”

The same message and the same speaker; the difference between the two cities was not in the one who spoke but in those who listened. A noble heart is not without doubts but lets the word in first and then examines it; a narrow heart shuts the door first and then looks for reasons.

We often think our problem is “not hearing enough,” when it is mostly “the wrong posture of hearing.” One who relies on his head, hearing a sermon, rebuts it in his heart with the first sentence; one who listens with the heart lets the word fall first and then discerns by the Holy Spirit. How noble a spiritual life is is measured not by how much one has read but by how far the heart is open to God’s word.
• What nobility looks like: hearing a piercing word, don’t defend first; first ask, “Lord, is this being said to me?”
• Heart, not head: receive first, then examine; not rebut first and then find reasons.
III. “Daily examining the Scriptures to see whether these things were so”—They Did Not Believe Paul; They Believed Scripture

Verse 11 (second half) and verse 12: “Daily examining the Scriptures to see whether these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, also of the Greek women of honorable estate, and not a few men.”

“Examining” in the original is a courtroom term, meaning to interrogate and cross-examine witnesses until a matter is thoroughly investigated. The Bereans did not merely look; they treated Paul’s words as testimony and checked them line by line against the Old Testament. “Daily”—not only on the Sabbath but every day. “To see whether these things were so”—they did not ask, “Does this man speak well?” but “Is this thing true?”

Paul was an apostle, and what he spoke was God’s revelation; yet he did not mind in the least that people checked him against Scripture. Truth does not fear examination; only the self fears it. A preacher who wants people to believe only him and not to check Scripture has already stepped into God’s place.

When a bank trains new tellers to spot counterfeit bills, it does not show them every kind of counterfeit; it has them handle genuine bills again and again. Once they know the real thing, a fake is known as soon as it is in the hand. Scripture is my standard means this: it is not that I can discern every error in the world, but that I am so familiar with God’s word that what does not agree feels wrong at once. This is what the Bereans relied on.

“Therefore”—because they examined, “many of them believed.” Examination did not block faith but gave birth to it; and this faith was rooted in Scripture, not in goodwill toward Paul. When Paul left, the faith remained.
• Daily, not only on the Lord’s Day: let Scripture be a book opened every day, not a weekend ornament.
• The one examined is myself: going home to open the Bible after a sermon, what I check is not only the speaker but whether what I believe is what God said.
IV. “Stirring up and troubling the multitudes” and “to go as far as to the sea”—The Enemy Followed, and Paul Went On Alone
Verses 13 to 15: the Jews of Thessalonica learned that Paul was preaching in Beroea and “came there likewise, agitating the multitudes.”

To walk fifty miles to another man’s city, not for the sake of their own city but to keep others from hearing the gospel. This is jealousy at its extreme: the self not only guards its own ground but pursues others to ruin theirs. “Stirring up and troubling”—one is inciting, the other agitating, like churning clear water into mud.

The brothers sent Paul away again, this time “to go as far as to the sea,” toward Athens. Silas and Timothy stayed, because the enemy’s target was Paul and the newborn church needed care. This was a mature arrangement: those who should go went, those who should stay stayed, neither retreating wholesale nor holding out wholesale.

“Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens”—the brothers of Beroea personally escorted him for hundreds of miles, a trip that with the return might take a month. These were people newly believing, doing this for a preacher who had stayed among them only a few weeks. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things—here it is not a doctrine but hundreds of miles of road.

Then Paul was left alone in Athens. He told Silas and Timothy to come “as soon as possible,” and those words reveal his state of mind—from Philippi until now he had had companions all the way, and now in a strange city full of idols he was alone. But he did not stop and wait; in the next devotion we will see what he did in the days of waiting.
• Recognize the source of agitation: when my heart is churned muddy, first ask whether this is the Holy Spirit’s illumination or the enemy’s stirring.

• Go when it is time to go, stay when it is time to stay: not every persecution must be held out against, and not every one must be retreated from; following the Holy Spirit’s guidance, those who go have peace and those who stay have peace.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Scripture Is My Standard
The Bereans said it in one word, making “Scripture is my standard” as clear as can be: examine.

In front of truth, a life of self most often does one of two things: either accepts everything as it comes because it is too lazy to check, or opposes everything because it does not want to change. The two look opposite, but their root is the same—the center is self: the first is my comfort, the second my own view. The Bereans were not like that. They “received the word with all eagerness,” which is self-denial—putting down preconceptions first and letting the word in; they “daily examined,” which is also self-denial—building faith not on goodwill toward a person but only on God’s word.

Humility is returning to one’s place. Man’s place is not judge of the truth but student of the truth. Paul was willing to be examined, and the Bereans were willing to examine, and neither stood above Scripture. In such a church, when the people leave, the word remains. Here is what it looks like today: of every sermon I have heard this week and every so-called “prompting,” have I really checked even one against Scripture? If not, what I believe may not be God’s word but only someone’s word.
a: See Off in the Night
Standing beside God’s servant in his most dangerous hour is the first ministry of a newborn church.
Receive First, Then Examine
When a piercing word comes, don’t defend first; first ask, “Lord, is this being said to me?”
Open the Bible Daily
Let God’s word be a book opened every day; know the real bill well and a fake is known at once.
Recognize the Agitation
When my heart is stirred up, first discern whether it is the Holy Spirit’s illumination or the enemy’s stirring.
Walk Further to See Someone Off
Going a few extra miles for others is what “people matter more than tasks” looks like.
q: When was the last time you heard a sermon or an exhortation and went home to check it against the Bible? For which saying will you do this this week?
How much of your faith is built on goodwill toward a certain preacher or spiritual elder? If that person left, would your faith still stand?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that in a mountain town off the highway You prepared a noble people. They were not smarter, only more open of heart; they did not believe Paul, they believed Your word. Thank You also that Your servant was willing to be examined, for truth never fears examination; only our selves do.
Lord, we confess that our posture in hearing is often wrong: what we like we accept as it comes, what we dislike we rebut first. Give us the heart of the Bereans, to receive with eagerness and examine daily; let our faith be built not on goodwill toward any person but only on Your word. When the enemy comes to agitate, give us a spirit of discernment, and give us the obedience to go when it is time to go and stay when it is time to stay. May Your word be the book we open each day and the standard of our whole lives. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who met him.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him. Some said, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preached Jesus and the resurrection.
They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which you are speaking about?
For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know therefore what these things mean.”
Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.
b: In the last devotion, the brothers of Beroea escorted Paul all the way to Athens, took his instructions that Silas and Timothy should come to him as soon as possible, and went back. Paul was left alone in Athens.

Athens was no ordinary city. Five hundred years earlier it had produced Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle; by Paul’s day the political center had long since moved to Rome, but Athens was still the university town and cultural capital of the whole empire. The Parthenon on the Acropolis and the colossal statue of Athena gleamed in the sun. A Jewish tentmaker stood alone in this city. What did he see?
I. “Now while Paul waited for them at Athens”—Days of Waiting, Not One of Them Empty
Verse 16 (first half): “Now while Paul waited for them at Athens.”

From a human point of view, these days were a gap—co-workers absent, no church. Yet Luke opens with “while Paul waited,” and what follows is a whole stretch of dense action: seeing, being distressed, reasoning, being brought to the Areopagus. Waiting in Paul was never a standstill.

We often treat “waiting” as days when nothing can be done: waiting for an answer, a door, a person. But the Lord guides in waiting just the same. The disciples waited for the Holy Spirit in the upper room, and those ten days were ten days of prayer; Paul waited in Athens for his co-workers, and those days became the preparation of a sermon that has lasted two thousand years.
• Waiting is not a gap: while waiting for a person or an answer, keep the eyes open and see what the Lord wants me to do now.
• Not a single day idle: what one does when there are no co-workers and no applause shows best what his life really is.
II. “He saw the city full of idols”—He Saw Not Art but Souls
Verse 16 (second half): “His spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols.”

“Full of idols” is one word in the original, meaning “swamped with idols.” The ancients said that Athens had more gods than people; in streets, temples, and on the columns of the marketplace, there were images of gods everywhere. A tourist arriving in Athens would see the peak of sculpture and the wonders of architecture; what Paul saw was a city bowing down to what does not exist.

“Provoked” in the original means “stirred up, stung,” the same root as the “contention” between Paul and Barnabas in chapter 15, and the word used in the Old Testament when God saw Israel worship idols and “burned with anger.” Paul’s spirit was stung—not because the idols were ugly but because they stole the glory that belonged to God.

On the same street two people walk by and see entirely different things: one sees property prices, another business opportunities, another people. What a person sees reveals what he holds in his heart. What Paul held in his heart was “let Jesus have all the glory,” so where glory was stolen he saw it at a glance, and seeing it hurt. This is not temper; it is focus.
• What do I see: entering a place, what do I notice first? That is what I hold in my heart.
• Hurt when glory is stolen: when God’s glory is given to something else, is there a sting in my heart? If not, perhaps I too have grown used to it.
III. “In the synagogue… and in the marketplace every day”—He Was Not Only Distressed, He Spoke

Verses 17 and 18: “So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also encountered him.”

After being distressed, what did Paul do? He opened his mouth. On the Sabbath in the synagogue, on other days “in the marketplace”—the agora of Athens, where Socrates had once questioned everyone he met. “Those who happened to be there” meant whoever he ran into, he talked to.

He met two schools of philosophers. The Epicureans held that pleasure is the highest good, that the gods, if they exist, are far away and do not concern themselves with people, and that when a man dies everything ends; the Stoics held that the universe has a reason, and that people should follow fate, restrain emotion, and stand on their own virtue. One said there is no judgment, the other said rely on yourself. These two voices have not disappeared today, only changed names: one is called “live for the moment,” the other “pull yourself up.”

Their verdict on Paul was cutting. “Babbler” in the original is “seed-picker,” a bird pecking scattered grains in the marketplace, extended to mean one who picks up other people’s words and patches them together with no real learning. “He seems to be advocating foreign deities”—hearing “Jesus” and “resurrection,” they supposed these were two new deities, a god and a goddess. They had not even understood, and already gave a verdict.
Paul did not shut his mouth because of this. The world’s best talkers mocked him as unable to talk, and he still spoke. The speaker can be looked down on; the message cannot.
• Distress must become speech: distress for people that does not speak will soon turn into complaint.
• Do not fear being despised: for one who speaks of Jesus to be called a “seed-picker” is normal; the message does not lose its power because the speaker is despised.
IV. “Brought to the Areopagus” and “telling or hearing some new thing”—A City That Loved Novelty

Verses 19 to 21: “They took hold of him, and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, ‘May we know what this new teaching is, which is spoken by you?’… Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.”

Areopagus originally meant “hill of Ares,” a small hill beside the Acropolis and also the name of Athens’ oldest council. That council handled matters of religion and morals, and anyone wanting to introduce new gods in Athens had to go through them. So Paul was brought there not to be arrested but to be asked to explain—a semi-formal hearing.

In verse 21 Luke adds a parenthetical comment with a touch of gentle irony: the Athenians “spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.” “New thing” in the original is “newer thing”—newer than new. This city had heard everything and feared only that there would be nothing new. What they asked Paul was not “Is this true?” but “Is this new?”

This is the greatest difference between Athens and Beroea. The Bereans, having heard, went to check the Scriptures to know “whether these things were so”; the Athenians, having heard, went to a meeting to know “what it means.” One puts truth into life, the other puts truth into the head.

The person who leans on himself with his head can discuss anything except change; for discussing is safe, and changing has a cost. Today we read a lot, hear a lot, and forward a lot, but “telling and hearing” is not “receiving eagerly.” If information stays in the head, however much one reads, life will not move an inch.
• Ask the right question: facing God’s word, am I asking “Is this true, and how must I change,” or “What is new about this”?
• From telling and hearing to doing: this week pick one truth already known, stop discussing it, and simply do it.
The Light of the 321 Principles: When the Focus Is on Jesus, the Eyes Can See
Everything Paul did in Athens began with a pair of eyes: he “saw” a city full of idols.

The Athenians saw those idols too, saw them every day until it was ordinary; the philosophers saw them as well, and saw art and tradition. Only Paul saw that they were idols, because his focus was on Jesus. A focus on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances—this decides what a person sees on entering a city, what he is distressed about, and whether he speaks.

A person of self entering Athens sees himself: I am alone, without co-workers, being mocked. A person emptied of self entering Athens sees the Lord: His glory is stolen here, His name is unknown here. The first waits until companions come before speaking; the second speaks in the days of waiting.

What letting Jesus have all the glory looks like today is simple: entering my office, my home, my group chat, do I see what is replacing Him there? Having seen, is there a sting? Having felt the sting, am I willing to speak?
a: No Standstill While Waiting
While waiting for an answer or a person, keep my eyes open and see what the Lord wants me to do now.
Check My First Glance
What I notice first on entering a place is what I hold in my heart.
Hurt When Glory Is Stolen
When God’s glory is given to something else, keep that sting in the heart alive.
Distress Must Become Speech
Don’t let distress for people turn into complaint against them.
From Discussion to Action
This week pick one truth already known, stop telling and hearing, and simply do it.
q: Think honestly: entering the place you know best—workplace, school, home—what do you usually notice first? What does that say about where your focus is?
Is there a truth you have heard many times and discussed often but never really done? What are you willing to do for it today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that though Your servant was alone in Athens, You did not let his waiting become a gap. Thank You for giving him eyes to see, in the most beautiful city in the world, Your glory being stolen, and a mouth to speak of Jesus and the resurrection even before the best talkers.
Lord, we confess that we often stand still while waiting, close our mouths where there are many people, and fail to see the idols in familiar places. Put Your focus back in our hearts, so that when we enter our homes, offices, and group chats, we can see what is replacing You and be distressed over it. And save us from the Athenians’ sickness, so that we do not treat Your word as a new thing to tell and hear but receive it eagerly and do it. May You receive all the glory in everything we see. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus, and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things.
For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you.
The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands.
He isn’t served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath, and all things.
He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons, and the boundaries of their dwellings,
that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us.
‘For in him we live, move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’
b: In the last devotion, the philosophers of Athens brought Paul to the Areopagus and asked him to explain what that “new teaching” meant. Luke even added a parenthetical remark: the Athenians spent their time in nothing else but telling or hearing some new thing.

Today Paul stood up. This is the only sermon in Acts addressed to purely Gentile intellectuals. His hearers had not read Moses and did not know David. Paul began from their city, their altar, their poets, and led them step by step before the God they did not know. Today’s reading is the first half of the sermon, on “who God is”; the next is the second half, on “what people should do.”
I. “I perceive that you are very religious” and “an Unknown God”—From What They Had to What They Lacked
Verses 22 and 23: Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things.”

“Religious” is a clever word; it can be praise—“you are very devout”—or criticism—“you are very superstitious.” Paul chose a word that works both ways as his opening, neither flattering nor offending. Then he spoke of something he had seen in the city: an altar inscribed “To an Unknown God.”

It really happened. Ancient writers record that Athens once suffered a plague that no sacrifice could stop, and someone proposed letting sheep loose and building an altar wherever a sheep lay down, dedicated to “the god no one knows”—lest they leave out a god and offend him. That altar was not faith but insurance. The Athenians worshiped thousands of gods and were still uneasy: might there be one more we do not know?
Paul cut in at exactly this unease: “What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I announce to you.” He did not say, “All you worship is false”; he began at the empty place already in their hearts.
• Begin with what the other already has: when talking faith with people, first see where in him the “uneasy” place is, and begin there.
• Neither flatter nor offend: observe and respect first, and when you speak, people can take it in.
II. “Does not dwell in temples made with hands, nor is he served by human hands”—God Does Not Need Us, Yet Gives Us Everything

Verses 24 and 25: “The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, neither is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath, and all things.”

Where Paul stood, lifting his head he could see the Parthenon. Before the building Athens was most proud of, he said that the God who made heaven and earth does not live in such a place. It was bold, yet it was the Old Testament’s constant teaching—Solomon said at the dedication of the temple, “Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27).

Then the second sentence: He is not “served by human hands, as though he needed anything.” This one turns the whole system of idols upside down. Idols need to be fed by people: offerings set out, incense burned, temples built, litters carried; without people, an idol is nothing. The true God is the opposite; He lacks nothing, and it is He who gives “life and breath and all things” to all. The very breath you are drawing now is His gift.

This is a deep reminder for our service. We often, without noticing, treat God as one who needs us: if I do not give myself, this work will not get done. It sounds responsible, but at bottom it magnifies the self. God does not lack me. That He lets me share in His work is grace, not need. Thinking this way, service does not wear one out into resentment, because I am not filling in for His lack but receiving His grace.
• God does not lack me: before serving, remember that He gives me breath, not that I give Him help.
• Grace, not need: change “He needs me to do it” to “He lets me share in it,” and resentment becomes gratitude.
III. “From one he made every nation of men” and “appointed seasons and boundaries”—Man Has a Place in God’s Hand
Verse 26: “He made from one every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons, and the boundaries of their dwellings.”

“From one” means from one man—Adam—He made all humanity. This sentence also grated in Athens. The Athenians had always prided themselves as an indigenous people “born from the soil,” and all other peoples as foreign barbarians. Paul said: no, you and the barbarians have the same source. Humanity has no noble or base bloodlines, only one Father.

“Having determined appointed seasons and boundaries”—when a nation rises and falls and which land it lives on are all in God’s hand. Assyria, Babylon, Greece, Rome—not one was an accident. This sentence is a warning to proud empires and a comfort to suffering peoples.

It is true at the personal level too. In which era and which family I was born—who decided that? Not I. This is exactly the starting point of humility—humility is not low self-esteem but returning to one’s place: let God be God and man be man. God sets the boundaries and man lives within them; pride is wanting to step beyond and determine for oneself everything one should have.
• I did not give birth to myself: from family background to era, nothing is something I earned; all were determined by Him.
• Live within my place: meeting a situation that cannot be changed today, first ask “why did He put me here,” not “how do I escape.”
IV. “If perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us”—Those Who Grope, and a God Near at Hand

Verses 27 and 28: “That they should seek God, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us; for in him we live, and move, and have our being. As some even of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’”

God made man, set the seasons, set the boundaries—for what purpose? “That they should seek God.” That emptiness in man which nothing can fill, that altar “to an Unknown God,” was placed there by God’s own hand, to bring people to look for Him.

“Reach out” in the original is “grope,” the way a blind man gropes in the dark. The religious history of all humanity is a history of groping: thousands of idols made, thousands of volumes of philosophy written, and still not found. But Paul followed with an extremely tender sentence: “though he is not far from each one of us.”

A child gropes in a house with the power out, frightened, crying loudly for his mother, when she is standing right beside him and he could touch her by reaching out. People do not find God not because God hides far away but because people grope with their eyes shut. Paul quoted their own poets—one saying “in him we live, and move, and have our being,” another “we are also his offspring”—even their poets had touched the edge: people live in God, as fish live in water.

This is exactly where Paul wanted to lead them: the God you do not know is not in the far-off stars or in temples made with hands; He is as near as can be—every breath you take is in Him. The question has never been whether He is there but whether you acknowledge Him.
• Stop groping: stop piecing together a god from my own reasoning; He is right here—open my eyes and acknowledge Him.
• Live in Him: every breath and every step today can be a sentence: “Lord, I know it is You.”
The Light of the 321 Principles: Let God Be God, and Man Be Man
The first half of the Areopagus sermon is really about one thing: God is God, and man is man.

God creates, God gives, God determines, God is near at hand; man is created, man receives, man lives within boundaries, man is to seek. This is the most basic order of the whole universe and also the root of all humanity’s problems—pride is leaving one’s place, man wanting to replace God: making gods himself (idols), feeding God himself (served by human hands), setting his own boundaries (my life, my decision). The Athenians worshiped thousands of gods, but at bottom it was people managing the gods; a life of self is the same—much prayer, but at bottom wanting God to do as I wish.

Humility is putting down power and returning to one’s place. What it looks like today: on opening my eyes in the morning, the first sentence is not “what will I do today” but “Lord, this breath is Yours, this day is determined by You, and I am in You.” When that sentence is said truly, a person returns to his place, and God is God in him.
a: Begin with What the Other Has
When talking faith with people, first find the “uneasy” place in his heart.
Remember God Does Not Lack Me
Change “He needs me to do it” to “He lets me share in it,” and resentment becomes gratitude.
Live in My Place
Facing a situation that cannot be changed, first ask, “Why did He put me here?”
Stop Groping
Stop piecing together a god from my own reasoning; open my eyes and acknowledge the Lord near at hand.
Acknowledge Him in Every Breath
In every moment of breathing, walking, and being today, say to the Lord, “I know it is You.”
q: Is there in your service a feeling that “God needs me, the church can’t do without me”? If you change it to “He lets me share in it,” what difference will it make to the weight in your heart?

Is there a situation you cannot change and do not want to accept—age, family, position? What does the sentence “having determined appointed seasons and boundaries” say to your heart in that situation?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are the God who made the world and all things in it, the Lord of heaven and earth. You do not dwell in temples made with hands, are not served by human hands, and lack nothing; rather You give life, breath, and all things to us. Every breath we take at this moment is from You.
Lord, we confess that we often leave our place. Like the Athenians, we make gods with our own thoughts, feed gods with our own hands, and want You to do as we wish; we also grope in the dark, crying out where You are, when You have been right beside us all along. Forgive our pride, and bring us back to man’s place, letting You be God. Let us live within the seasons and boundaries You have determined without struggle, and let us recognize You in every breath. May our living, moving, and being truly be in You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man.
The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent,
because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.”
Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.”
Thus Paul went out from among them.
But certain men joined with him and believed, among whom also was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
b: In the last devotion, Paul gave the first half of his speech on the Areopagus: the God who made heaven and earth does not dwell in temples made with hands, is not served by human hands, gives life and breath to all, is not far from each one of us, and in Him we live, and move, and have our being. Even Athens’ poets said that we are His offspring.

Today is the second half. The first half spoke of “who God is,” and the hearers could perhaps still nod; the second half speaks of “what people should do,” and Paul said the three words the Athenians least wanted to hear: repent, judgment, resurrection. When a sermon reaches here, the assembly divides into three kinds of people.
I. “We ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone”—A God Made by Man Is Man Enlarged
Verse 29: “Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and device of man.”

Paul first drew a conclusion from the previous verse. Since we are God’s offspring, God is of course greater than we are; how could a God greater than I be one I carved with “art” and “device”? “Art” is skill in the hands, “device” is imagination in the mind—idols are the product of these two: man first thinks up in his head what a god should look like, then makes it with his hands.

This sentence is not far from us. The essence of an idol lies not in its material but in its source: any “god I thought up” is an idol. Some have a god in the heart whose only job is to make things go smoothly for them, some a god who never rebukes, some a god who takes their side—those are carved with “device.” A god made by man is, in the end, man enlarged.

Scripture is my standard exists to deal with this. Who God is is not for me to think up but for Him to say; my responsibility is not to carve a god to my liking but to know, in His word, the God who simply is.
• Examine the idols in the heart: how much of my knowledge of God is what Scripture says, and how much is what I wish He were?
• Let God say who He is: when reading Scripture, meeting a God not to my liking, don’t skip it; that is exactly when the idol is torn down.
II. “The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent”—Repentance Is Changing Glasses
Verse 30: “The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent.”

“Overlooked” in the original is “looked past without pursuing,” which does not mean God did not care but that He was patient. But “now”—this word cuts history in two. Jesus has come, died, and risen. Before, one could say “I did not know”; now one cannot. God is no longer only patient; He gives a command: “all people everywhere should repent.” Everywhere, no exception; all, no exemption.

“Repent” in the original means “to change one’s mind,” to take a different view, a different direction. It is not only grief over wrong done but the whole person turning around—from facing away from God to facing Him. A changed way of thinking changes a life, and a changed life changes how one lives; repentance begins exactly with thinking: from man’s view to God’s view, from earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal.

A person who has worn glasses of the wrong prescription for years sees everything crooked and assumes the world is just that way. Repentance is putting on the right glasses: the world has not changed; he sees what is true. So repentance is not God wanting people to suffer but God wanting people to see clearly.
And God does not “suggest” this; He “commands” it. The Athenians were used to discussing everything, but this sentence is not for discussion; it is for obedience.
• Repentance begins with thinking: is there something today I have always viewed from my own viewpoint that the Lord wants me to change to His?
• A command is not a suggestion: facing God’s word, am I “considering” or “obeying”?
III. “He has appointed a day,” “the man whom he has ordained,” and “raised him from the dead… given assurance”—One Day, One Man, One Proof

Verse 31: “Because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.”
Why repent? Because there is judgment. This verse holds three things: an appointed day, an ordained man, and a trustworthy assurance.

“He has appointed a day”—judgment is not “possible” but “already” on the calendar. The day is set, only not announced; like an exam date already printed in the school calendar, whether you study is up to you, but the day will not be postponed because you are unprepared. “Judge the world in righteousness”—not by man’s standard, not by anyone’s power, but by righteousness. This is a comfort to the wronged and a warning to the self-righteous.

“By the man whom he has ordained”—the Judge is a man. Paul had not yet spoken Jesus’ name, but the whole assembly knew whom he meant. “Raised him from the dead, given assurance to all men”—the resurrection is God’s proof to all humanity: this is the one I have ordained.

Notice Paul’s order. He did not begin with “believe in Jesus and you will be happy”; he said: there is judgment, the Judge is appointed, the proof is the resurrection, therefore repent. The gospel does not begin with benefits; it begins with truth.
• The day is set: every decision I make today will have to stand before that day.
• The resurrection is the proof: what I believe is not a comfort but a fact God has sealed.
IV. “Mocked,” “We want to hear you again about this,” and “joined him and believed”—Three Kinds of People, One Fruit

Verses 32 to 34: “Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, ‘We want to hear you again concerning this.’ Thus Paul went out from among them. But certain men joined with him, and believed…”

The Athenians could accept a Creator God, could accept that people are God’s offspring, and could even accept judgment—but when it came to “resurrection from the dead,” the assembly changed. Greek philosophy had always held that the body is the soul’s prison and that escaping the body at death is release, so why would anyone want to return to a body? So some “mocked,” turning up their noses.

The second kind were more polite: “We want to hear you again concerning this.” It sounded interested but meant “some other day”—that telling-and-hearing the Athenians did best. They did not reject the truth; they put it on the schedule of a next time that never comes.

The third kind: “certain men joined with him, and believed.” “Joined” means stuck on, following closely. Among them were Dionysius the Areopagite—a member of the very council that had questioned Paul—and a woman named Damaris. One was an insider of the establishment and the other a woman; in Athens, either believing cost a great deal.

By human eyes this sermon was a failure: no numbers, no church, and not a single “letter to the Athenians” in the New Testament. But Luke recorded “certain men” and their names. God’s work is not counted by numbers; in the hardest city, a few who joined the Lord were the fruit.
• Which kind am I: facing the part of God’s word least to my liking, do I mock, say “some other day,” or join?
• Don’t measure fruit by numbers: one person truly turned to the Lord means a sermon was not preached in vain.
The Light of the 321 Principles: A Changed Way of Thinking Changes Life

Paul’s sermon in Athens half tore down and half built up. What it tore down was the god man made by art and device; what it built up was the God who appointed a day, ordained a man, and gave the resurrection as proof. The word in the middle is repent—change the mind.

Why is it hard for a life of self to repent? Because repenting means admitting that I saw wrongly before, and that is exactly what the self least wants to admit. So the person of self mocks (what you say is wrong) and delays (another time), and simply will not join. Self-denial is not having no views but being willing to let God’s view replace mine; what that looks like today is: when Scripture and my view conflict, I change my view, not Scripture’s interpretation.

Change begins with me. Athens had no revival, but Dionysius changed, and Damaris changed. God’s system has never begun with a city; it begins with a few who are willing to change glasses. Today, am I among those few?
a: Tear Down the God Made by Device
Examine how much of my knowledge of God is what I wish He were.
Repentance Begins with Thinking
Find one matter I have always viewed from my own viewpoint and change it to God’s.
A Command Is Not a Suggestion
Facing God’s word, move from “considering” to “obeying.”
Remember the Day Is Set
Every decision today will have to stand before that day.
Join, Don’t Delay
Don’t put truth on a “next time” that never comes; turn to Him today.
q: Is there a passage of Scripture you have always put off hearing “some other day” and never really faced? Today, are you willing to move it from “next time” to “this time”?
Think of something you recently insisted on your own way: if God’s view differs from yours, would you change your view, or find an interpretation that lets God agree with you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are not a god carved by our art and device but the One who simply is. Thank You for being patient while people were in ignorance and now commanding us to repent; and thank You for raising Jesus from the dead as a trustworthy assurance, so that we know the day of judgment is set and the Judge has been appointed.
Lord, we confess that the shadow of the Athenians is in us: what suits us we hear, what does not we mock or say “some other day.” Tear down the idols we have made in our own thinking, so that in Your word we may know You as You are. Give us a heart of repentance, willing to put on Your glasses, to change from man’s view to Your view, from the temporary to the eternal. Make us, like Dionysius and Damaris, not only hear but join You and believe in You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth.

He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them,
and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.
He reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath and persuaded Jews and Greeks.
But when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.
When they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his clothing and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!”
