He departed there, and went into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized.
The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent;
for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
b: In the last devotion, the sermon on the Areopagus ended in mockery and “some other day,” and only a few joined Paul and believed. Athens did not keep a church.

Today Paul walked west about fifty miles to Corinth. This passage has no riot and no prison, but it has an apostle’s weakest hour and one sentence the Lord spoke to him by night. And this city’s church began in a tent-making workshop.
I. “He departed from Athens and came to Corinth”—From the Cultural Capital to the Port of Vice
Verse 1: “After these things he departed from Athens, and came to Corinth.”

Athens was a university town; Corinth was a commercial port. It sat on the isthmus joining northern and southern Greece, with a harbor on each side, so that goods went overland across the isthmus instead of sailing around the peninsula. Many people, much money, travelers of every sort; the city had every kind of religion and a temple of the goddess of love. The Greeks coined a verb, “to Corinthianize,” meaning to live in debauchery. It was the capital of the province of Achaia, far larger than Athens and far dirtier.

What was Paul like as he entered this city? Later he himself said, “I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). This was no victorious hero entering a city, but a man who had just come out of the coldness of Athens with not one co-worker beside him. Apostles too have low points, and Scripture does not cover for him.
• The Lord’s servant also has times of weakness: trembling is not failure but a person at the end of himself.
• The Lord goes even to the dirtiest city: God works not only in halls of culture but also in the marketplace of the port.
II. “They were tent makers by trade”—God Prepared a Co-Worker in a Workshop
Verses 2 and 3: Paul met Aquila and Priscilla, “because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome,” and they had recently come from Italy.

Roman historians record that in AD 49 the Emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of constant disturbances over a certain “Chrestus.” One expulsion order pushed a married couple to Corinth; Paul, left cold in Athens, also walked to Corinth. Two roads pushed by circumstances met in a tent-making workshop.

“Tent making” was leatherwork, a craft Paul had learned in Tarsus as a boy. Being “of the same trade,” “he lived with them and worked.” In his first months in Corinth, by day Paul was a craftsman sewing leather at a workbench, and only on the Sabbath a preacher. This couple later became his most important co-workers; he said that they “for my life, laid down their own necks” (Romans 16:4).

God’s preparation is often not a miracle dropped from heaven but a couple driven from home, a craft that puts bread on the table, and a workbench. People matter more than tasks—the first thing Paul gained in Corinth was not a pulpit but a home.
• See God’s preparation: that person beside me of the same trade, same workplace, same road may be exactly the co-worker God prepared for me.
• A craft is also ministry: working honestly at the workbench and preaching at the pulpit are the same person serving the same Lord.
III. “Compelled by the word” and “shook out his clothing”—Having Done His Duty, He Turned

Verses 4 to 6: Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, and brought the gifts of the Macedonian churches (2 Corinthians 11:9). With co-workers and provision, Paul stood up from the workbench and “was compelled by the word”—in the original, “seized by the word,” his whole being pressed and urged by that message, preaching full time.

The result was “opposed and blasphemed.” Paul “shook out his clothing”—a Jewish gesture, like Nehemiah shaking out the fold of his garment (Nehemiah 5:13), meaning “I have shaken your responsibility off.” “Your blood be upon your own heads”—from Ezekiel: if the watchman warns and the hearer does not listen, the blood is on the hearer’s own head and the watchman is clear (Ezekiel 33:4–5).

Paul was not sulking. He was saying: I have done my duty as watchman; your choice is yours. Here is a healthy boundary: I am responsible to people, but not for people’s choices. The person of self cannot tell these two apart and either presses people to the end or blames himself to the end; the person emptied of self, having spoken clearly and committed the result to God, turns to do the next thing the Lord wants.
• Do my duty, don’t carry the result: I have said what I should and done what I should, and how the other chooses I commit to God.
• Turning is not giving up: going from the synagogue to the Gentiles is changing direction by the Holy Spirit’s guidance, not storming off.
IV. “His house was next door to the synagogue” and “Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue”—The Door Was Next Door

Verses 7 and 8: Paul left the synagogue—where did he go? Next door. Titius Justus was a God-fearing Gentile, and his house was “next door to the synagogue,” perhaps wall against wall. He did not hide at the other end of the city but kept speaking right beside the synagogue; every Sabbath, those going in and out of the synagogue could see the door next door standing open.

Then the most incredible thing happened: “Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house.” The ruler of the synagogue was the person of highest standing in that community; when he believed, he led his whole household through that next-door gate (1 Corinthians 1:14 says Paul baptized him himself). Then “many of the Corinthians, hearing, believed, and were baptized.”
Paul was opposed in the synagogue and gained the ruler of the synagogue next door. When God closes one door, the one He opens is often right next door.
• The door is often next door: when rejected, don’t go far at first; see which door God opened beside you.
• Fruit in unexpected people: the place of most resistance may produce the firmest believer.
V. “Don’t be afraid, but speak” and “I have many people in this city”—The Lord Spoke by Night

Verses 9 to 11: why did the Lord say “don’t be afraid” at this moment? Because Paul was afraid. Experience told him what would happen next: Philippi was prison, Thessalonica a riot, Beroea a pursuit. With the ruler of the synagogue believing, the counterattack would be fiercer still. He was probably already thinking about packing up the tents.

The Lord said four things. “Don’t be afraid”—dealing with the feeling; “speak and don’t be silent”—dealing with the action; “I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you”—dealing with the situation; and then the deepest sentence: “I have many people in this city.”

“I have”—before they had believed, the Lord already called them “my people.” What Paul saw was opposition and blasphemy; what the Lord saw was a people not yet found. This is the foundation of building God’s system: it is not that we make God’s people, but that God already has His people and we go to find them.
So Paul stayed a year and six months. A frightened man wanted to leave; the Lord’s word made him stay; and in those eighteen months, the church of Corinth was born.
• Deal with fear first: the Lord gave Paul not a strategy first but “don’t be afraid”; in my service today, is there something where fear is making the decision?
• See my city with the Lord’s eyes: what I see is resistance; what He sees is people not yet found.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Lord Sees His People, I See My Fear

These eleven verses are a process from weakness to standing firm. When Paul entered the city he was “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling”; eighteen months later he had built a church there. It was not that he became strong but that the Lord spoke to him in the night.

In a hard city, a life of self sees itself: my situation, my fear, my past wounds. With the focus on self, a person wants to leave. Self-denial is not having no feelings—Paul’s fear was real; it is moving the focus from my fear to the Lord’s word—“I am with you,” “I have many people in this city.” Once the focus moves, the same city turns from a city to flee into a field the Lord wants to harvest.

Follow the Holy Spirit with the heart, rather than lean on yourself with the head. Paul calculating with his head could not stay in Corinth; when the Lord had him listen with his heart, he stayed. What it looks like today: when I want to leave in a difficulty, don’t decide first; first be quiet and listen to what the Lord is saying about this place.
a: Admit Weakness
Trembling is not failure; apostles too have low points—bring it before the Lord.
See the Co-Worker Beside Me
That person of the same trade, workplace, or road today may be the Aquila God prepared.
Do My Duty, Don’t Carry the Result
Having said what I should, commit the other’s choice to God and turn to the next thing.
The Door Is Next Door
When rejected, don’t go far at first; see which door God opened beside me.
Let the Lord’s Word Overcome Fear
In the place I want to flee, listen quietly while the Lord says, “I have many people in this city.”
q: Is there a place you now want to “leave”—a job, a fellowship, a relationship? Before deciding, quietly ask the Lord: Are You saying to me “go,” or “stay, I have people here”?
Think of the “Aquilas and Priscillas” around you—ordinary people of the same trade and the same road. Have you seen that they may be the co-workers God prepared for you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your servant entered Corinth in weakness and trembling, and You prepared a co-worker for him in a tent-making workshop, opened a door for him next to the synagogue, and spoke to him in person by night. Thank You that even in the most debauched city You had many people, and that before we knew You, You already called us Yours.
Lord, we confess that in hard places we often see only our own fear, the opposition, and our past wounds, and want to pack up the tents and leave. Say to us also: don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent, for You are with us. Give us Your eyes, so that in our homes, workplaces, and cities we see Your people not yet found. Give us the freedom to do our duty without carrying the result, and the patience not to go far from the door next door. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.”
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you;
but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.”
So he drove them from the judgment seat.
Then all the Greeks seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.
b: In the last devotion, the Lord said to Paul by night, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent; for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.” So Paul stayed in Corinth a year and six months.

The Lord’s promise was “no one will attack you to harm you,” not “no one will attack you.” Today’s passage is when the attack came. The Jews dragged Paul into court, but this time, before he had said a word, the matter was over. The one who defended him was a Roman official with no interest in the gospel.
I. “When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia”—One Name Pins Scripture to History

Verses 12 and 13: “But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him to the judgment seat, saying, ‘This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.’”

Gallio was no minor figure. He was the elder brother of the Roman philosopher Seneca, who praised him as “so gentle to everyone.” In the early twentieth century archaeologists found at Delphi in Greece a stone inscription bearing a decree of the Emperor Claudius, mentioning Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, which can be dated to AD 51–52. This verse became a nail in the chronology of the whole New Testament: the dates of Paul in Corinth are calculated from Gallio.

“Judgment seat” in the original is the “bema,” and in the square of ancient Corinth today that stone platform is still there. The Jews “with one accord rose up”—this was their first collective action in over a year, evidently timed for when the new proconsul had just taken office and was not yet familiar with local affairs.

The accusation was clever: “persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.” Which law? If Jewish law, a Roman official would not care; if heard as Roman law, it meant that Paul was preaching an unapproved religion. They left it vague so that Gallio would misunderstand.
• Scripture stands in history: what we believe is no legend but a fact whose dates can be checked against a stone.
• Attacks pick their timing: the enemy does not come at any time but waits for when you are least prepared; so alertness cannot be only for smooth times.
II. “Just as Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said”—He Did Not Have to Say a Word
Verse 14: “But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, ‘If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you.’”

Paul was ready. He had spoken on the Areopagus and reasoned in synagogues; standing before the proconsul this time, he had a whole speech to give. But just as he “was about to open his mouth,” Gallio spoke. Paul’s defense was not used by a single word.

Sometimes our best defense is God not letting us speak. Had Paul spoken, it would have become “the Jews against Paul”; with Gallio speaking first, it became “Rome against the Jews.” God used an unbelieving official to do what Paul himself could not. How was “no one will attack you to harm you,” said by the Lord in the night, fulfilled? Not by Paul’s eloquence, not by an angel appearing, but by a proconsul’s impatience. The fulfillment of God’s promise often looks different from what we imagine.

With the self, the greatest fear is “no chance to explain,” always feeling that if I just made it clear, others would understand. A person emptied of self knows that there is a kind of defense that needs no opening of the mouth—close the mouth and see what God does. What it looks like today: when misunderstood, don’t rush to send a message of explanation; first pray, and see whether the Lord wants me to speak.
• Let God speak first: when misunderstood, first ask the Lord, “This time, do You want me to open my mouth or keep it shut?”
• Promises are not fulfilled as I imagine: God said “no one will harm you,” and He can accomplish it through an unbeliever.
III. “Look to it yourselves! I don’t want to be a judge of these matters”—A Cold Remark Became a Protective Door
Verses 15 and 16: “But if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.” And he drove them from the judgment seat.

Gallio saw through it. He said: if it is “a matter of wrong or wicked crime”—real crime—I would certainly hear it; but what you are quarreling over is “words and names and your own law,” an internal matter of your religion, and I will not judge it. “Drove them from the judgment seat” is a very unceremonious action.

The significance of this ruling was greater than anyone then saw. Roman law protected Judaism; Gallio in effect declared that what Christians believe belongs to an internal Jewish dispute and is therefore equally protected by law. This was the empire’s first legal stance on the gospel, and a favorable one; for the next dozen years or so, officials in various places largely followed this precedent. A philosopher’s elder brother, out of impatience, held up an umbrella over the gospel.

Gallio did not love the Lord, did not believe the gospel, and may even have looked down on the whole affair. Yet God used him. We often pray for a good environment, good officials, good bosses; but God does not necessarily change the environment; He can, in an unchanged environment, open a door through an unbeliever.
• God uses whom He will use: even a person with no interest in the gospel can become a vessel by which God protects the church.
• Don’t seek a good environment; seek to see God: a cold environment does not mean God is absent; He often works right in the coldness.
IV. “They all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat”—The World’s Indifference, and a Man Beaten
Verse 17: “Then they all took hold of Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.”

The accusers were driven out and in turn became the ones beaten. “They all” were probably the Greeks in the square, who disliked the Jews anyway, and seeing the proconsul not on the Jews’ side, seized the chance to act. The one beaten was “Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue”—the new head of the synagogue who took over after Crispus believed, very likely the one who led this accusation.

“Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.” This sentence has two layers. One is that he was just: he would not intervene in internal religious affairs because someone was being beaten. The other is indifference: a man was beaten before his own seat and he was unmoved. Roman justice and Roman indifference were the same man. The world can protect the gospel, but the world does not love the gospel.

It is interesting that when Paul later wrote 1 Corinthians, he began, “Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes” (1 Corinthians 1:1). If this is the same man, then the one who led the accusation against Paul before the court and was beaten by the crowd became, a few years later, Paul’s “brother.” God not only protected Paul but may also have gained the man who accused him.
• The world’s protection is not love: don’t take an official’s justice for the gospel’s friend, and don’t take indifference for hostility; the Lord works in ways beyond both.
• Today’s beater may be tomorrow’s brother: leave a door open for those who persecute you.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Focus Is on Jesus, Not on the Environment

In these six verses Paul hardly acts: dragged up, about to open his mouth, and then dismissed. The subjects of the whole passage are the Jews, Gallio, and the crowd—anyone but Paul. Yet what the Lord said in the night was fulfilled word for word: “no one will attack you to harm you.”

The person of self in such a situation will strain to do something himself: to defend, to explain, to find connections, because the self believes the outcome is in my hands. Self-denial is not passivity; Paul did not flee, and he stood in court ready to speak; self-denial is, after doing one’s part, handing over the result—when God wants him to speak, he speaks; when God has another speak, he is silent. What it looks like today: facing an unjust misunderstanding, after giving the explanation I should, I no longer argue my case again and again, and let God vindicate me in His own way.

The focus is on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances. Gallio was cold, the crowd was rough, the Jews were hostile—none of the circumstances was good, yet the Lord’s word stood. Letting Jesus be King is not only in favorable times but also in court and under attack, trusting that the King is still on the throne.
a: Believe a Faith with Dates
God’s works are pinned in history, can be checked, and withstand examination.
Let God Speak First
When misunderstood, first ask the Lord whether to open or close my mouth, and don’t rush to explain myself.
Recognize Whom God Uses
A person cold to the gospel may be the vessel by which God opens a door.
Don’t Mistake Indifference for Hostility
The world does not love the gospel, but the Lord can work in the coldness.
Leave a Door for Those Who Strike You
The Sosthenes who accuses you today may be your brother tomorrow.
q: Think of something you were recently misunderstood about. Could it be that the Lord wants you to keep your mouth shut and let Him speak? Are you willing today to stop explaining and first pray?
In your life, is there a “Gallio”—someone cold to faith who helped you at a critical time? Have you thanked God for him?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that what You said to Paul in the night was fulfilled word for word in court. You used no angel and no miracle; You used an unbelieving proconsul who, before Your servant had opened his mouth, closed the door and opened it. Your promises are not fulfilled as we imagine, yet they never fail.
Lord, we confess that when misunderstood we are always in a hurry to explain and to defend, as though the result were in our hands. Teach us, like Paul, to stand firm and also to keep our mouths shut; having done our part, to commit the result to You. Move our focus from circumstances back to You, so that in cold environments we see Your hand. And give us a wide heart, to leave a door open for those who attack us today, for You can make those who accuse us into brothers. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Paul, having stayed after this many more days, took his leave of the brothers,  and sailed from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow.
He came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself entered into the synagogue, and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay with them a longer time, he declined;
but taking his leave of them, he said, “I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return again to you if God wills.” Then he set sail from Ephesus.
When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch.
Having spent some time there, he departed, and went through the region of Galatia, and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples.
Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him, and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace;
for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.
b: In the last devotion, Gallio drove the accusing Jews from the judgment seat, Sosthenes was beaten before it, and Gallio cared about none of it. The Lord’s word was fulfilled: no one would harm Paul.

Today’s passage moves quickly: Paul left Corinth, passing through Ephesus, Caesarea, Jerusalem, and Antioch; the second journey ended and the third began. Then the camera turns, and a new figure walks into Ephesus—a man highly eloquent and fervent in heart, yet knowing only half. Today we look at an apostle who knew when to go, and a couple who knew how to help a person along.
I. “He had made a vow,” and “had his hair cut in Cenchreae”—An Apostle’s Thanksgiving

Verse 18: “Paul, having stayed after this many more days, took his leave of the brothers, and sailed from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He had his hair cut in Cenchreae, for he had a vow.”

Cenchreae was a harbor east of Corinth. Paul cut his hair here because he “had a vow.” This was very likely the Nazirite vow of the Old Testament (Numbers 6): out of thanksgiving or petition, a person for a period would not cut his hair or drink wine, and at its end would cut his hair and offer a sacrifice. When did Paul make the vow? Probably in those most fearful days in Corinth, when the Lord said to him in the night, “Don’t be afraid.” Now eighteen months had passed, not one of the Lord’s words had fallen to the ground, and he cut his hair, returning this stretch of days to God.

We often think of Paul as one opposed to the law, yet here he himself kept a Jewish vow. He was not bound by the law but used the way most familiar to his own people to express thanks to God. It was the act of one who, having finished a stretch of road, turned back to say “thank you” to God.
• Give thanks for a finished stretch: when something ends, don’t rush on to the next; first stop and return it to God.
• Thanks needs an action: not only feeling grateful inside; find a visible way to express it to God.
II. “He did not consent” and “If God wills”—An Open Door He Did Not Enter

Verses 19 to 21: “They came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself entered into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay with them a longer time, he didn’t consent, but taking his leave of them, and saying, ‘I will return again to you if God wills.’”

Ephesus was the capital of the province of Asia, the fourth largest city of the empire, where at the start of the second journey the Holy Spirit had forbidden Paul to preach (16:6). Now he finally came, and on entering the synagogue the Jews even “asked him to stay a longer time”—rare in Paul’s experience. The door was open, the people welcomed him, but he “didn’t consent.”

Why? He did not explain, saying only, “I will return again to you if God wills.” Some think he was hurrying to Jerusalem for a feast, others that he had to report in Antioch first. Whatever the reason, he was clear on one thing: a door being open does not mean it is time to enter now. The Holy Spirit is my guide, not only guiding people to detour when a door is closed but also guiding them to go on first when a door is open.

This is a hard lesson for us. Our rule is often “seize the opportunity,” but Paul’s rule was “if God wills.” He left Ephesus in the hands of Priscilla and Aquila—leaving his two most trusted co-workers there and going first himself. Later he did come back and stayed three years in Ephesus. The work of those three years was what this couple laid down first.
• Ask even when the door is open: with a good opportunity before me, first ask “if God wills,” not “can I seize it.”
• Leaving people matters more than leaving myself: Paul left, yet left his best co-workers; the system is built by those who stay.
III. “Greeted the assembly” and “strengthening all the disciples”—One Journey Ended, Another Began with Relationships

Verses 22 and 23: “When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch. After he had spent some time there, he departed, and went through the region of Galatia, and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples.”

In two verses, over a thousand miles. “Went up and greeted the assembly” in Jerusalem—he reported to the church that had sent him; “went down to Antioch”—he returned to the mother church from which he set out. The second journey was over. “After he had spent some time there, he departed”—and so the third journey began, Luke saying not one more word.

The first thing on the third journey was the same as the second: “strengthening all the disciples.” “In order,” place after place, not one disciple left out. Each time Paul set out, he did not first open new ground but first went back to see the old disciples. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—he valued relationships above pioneering.
• Go back to see the old disciples: before opening something new, first look back at how those already led are doing.
• Greeting is ministry: for the church that sent and raised you, going back to report and greet is not formality but relationship.
IV. “An eloquent man,” “fervent in spirit,” and “knowing only the baptism of John”—A Very Good Man, but Not Complete

Verses 24 and 25: “Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures. This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.”

Alexandria was the second largest city of the empire, with the greatest library of the time, where Jews had translated the Old Testament into Greek. Apollos was a scholar from such a city: “eloquent” (also rendered “learned”), “mighty in the Scriptures”—a man who could both speak and understood the Scriptures. And he was “fervent in spirit”—in the original, “boiling in spirit”—and spoke of Jesus “accurately.”

But there is one “though”: “he knew only the baptism of John.” He knew who Jesus was, but probably did not know that after Pentecost the Holy Spirit had been poured out, or that those who believe in Jesus are to be baptized in His name and receive the Holy Spirit. He had fire, learning, and accurate content, lacking only one piece—and the missing piece was the very core of Acts.

There are many such people today: they have read a lot, speak well, and truly love the Lord, yet one piece in their life has not been touched by the Holy Spirit. Gifts and learning can cover this gap for a long time, others cannot see it, and the person himself may not know.
• Having fire is not being complete: zeal and eloquence cover gaps; ask the Lord to point out my “though.”
• Learning is a gift, not a guarantee: however well I speak, I must ask, “Have I myself experienced what I am speaking?”
V. “Took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately”—What Helping a Person Looks Like

Verses 26 to 28: “He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately. When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him, and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace; for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.”
This couple did three things, each worth learning.

First, they did not correct him publicly in the synagogue. “Took him aside”—they invited him to their home to eat. A person’s gap is to be mended in a relationship, not exposed from a platform. Second, they “explained more accurately”—not saying “you were wrong” but “there is more.” What they supplied was what Apollos lacked, not a denial of what he already had. Third, once mended, they let go: Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, and the brothers wrote to recommend him. They did not keep this highly eloquent man for their own Ephesus.

And Apollos too is admirable. A scholar from Alexandria, he was willing to sit and hear a couple of tent makers explain the Scriptures. This is what humility looks like today: however much I know, willing to let someone of lower standing tell me what I still lack.

Every string on a violin is good, but if one is tuned off, the whole piece goes out of tune; tuning is not replacing the instrument but gently tightening that one string. This is what Priscilla and Aquila did. Apollos, once tuned, arrived in Corinth and “greatly helped those who had believed through grace,” and Paul later said, “I planted, Apollos watered” (1 Corinthians 3:6).
• Mend at home, don’t expose on the stage: seeing a brother’s gap, first invite him to a meal, not correct him publicly.
• Let someone of lower standing teach me: true learning is being willing to have a tent maker explain to me more accurately.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Only Self-Denial Can Bring Unity—Those Who Teach and Those Who Learn Must Both Deny Self

This passage has two kinds of letting go. Paul let go: the door of Ephesus stood open, and he did not enter but handed it to co-workers; Apollos let go: his learning and eloquence were right there, yet he let two lay people fill what he lacked. And Priscilla and Aquila let go too: they sent the mended man on, not keeping him for themselves.

The person of self cannot do these three things. The person of self seizes any opportunity, guards any learning, and keeps any talent. Self-denial is not having no gifts and no judgment but that gifts and judgment are no longer under my own management—Jesus is King, and I listen for Him to say “allow” or “don’t allow.” What it looks like today: when a good opportunity comes, ask God first, not whether I can seize it; when a correction comes, listen first, not whether the speaker is qualified enough; when a good talent is in my hands, ask the Lord first where He wants that person to go, not what he can do for me.

Only such a people can build God’s system. A system is not held up by one capable person but by a couple willing to take someone home and explain more accurately, a scholar willing to be explained to, and an apostle willing to leave the door to others—each emptied of self, they are naturally one.
a: Give Thanks for a Finished Road
When something ends, first stop and return it to God, then go on to the next.
Ask God Even When the Door Is Open
With a good opportunity before me, first ask “if God wills,” not “can I seize it.”
Go Back to See the Old Disciples
Before opening something new, look back at how those already led are doing.
Ask the Lord to Show Me My “Though”
Zeal and eloquence cover gaps; let the Holy Spirit point out that piece.
Mend People at Home
Seeing a brother’s lack, first invite him home to explain more accurately, and don’t correct him publicly.
q: Is there a “though” in your life—a place covered by zeal and gifts but not yet touched by the Holy Spirit? Whom are you willing to let “explain more accurately” to you?
Is there a door now standing open before you that you want to seize? Before seizing it, have you first asked “if God wills”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your servant, having finished a stretch of road, cut his hair and fulfilled his vow, was willing to go on first even when a door was open, and began again with relationships when one journey ended. Thank You also for giving a couple like Priscilla and Aquila, who had no pulpit but at home explained more accurately to a learned man, and then let go so that he could go on.
Lord, we confess that we seize every opportunity, guard every scrap of learning, and keep every talent; we also confess that our zeal and eloquence often cover the “though” in our lives. Give us Paul’s obedience, to ask first in everything, “if God wills”; give us Apollos’ humility, willing to let those of lower standing tell us what we still lack; and give us the gentleness of Priscilla and Aquila, who, seeing a brother’s gap, first bring him home and do not expose him on the stage. May each of us deny self, so that Your church may be one, the system You build. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples.
He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
He said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.”
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them and they spoke with other languages and prophesied.
They were about twelve men in all.
b: In the last devotion, Paul returned to Antioch for a while, then set out again and went through Galatia and Phrygia. During the same period, a man named Apollos appeared in Ephesus, “mighty in the Scriptures,” fervent in spirit, “though he knew only the baptism of John.” Priscilla and Aquila took him home and explained the way of God to him more accurately, and he crossed over to Achaia.

Luke begins with the words “while Apollos was at Corinth” because he wants us to see two things side by side: Apollos had stopped at the baptism of John, and the men Paul meets in Ephesus have stopped in the very same place. The last devotion was about one man whose gap was filled; this one is about twelve. The city of Ephesus began with a group of people who were “one step short.”
I. “Having passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus”—Returning to the Place He Had Promised

“The upper country” refers to the inland highlands of Asia Minor. Paul did not take the trade road along the river valley; he went by the hill country, through Galatia and Phrygia, and finally came down from the heights to the coastal city of Ephesus. At the end of his second journey he had stayed there briefly. The Jews asked him to remain longer, and he declined, leaving only these words: “I will return again to you if God wills” (18:21). Now he has come back.

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, with a population of about 250,000. The Temple of Artemis in the city was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world; priests, pilgrims, silversmiths and sorcerers made up a vast religious economy. If the gospel was to reach all of Asia, Ephesus was the gate it had to pass through. Paul would stay here three years—the longest he ever stayed in any one city. God’s servant is not always running; sometimes he makes us stop so that a place can be built up solidly.
• Remember what you have said: “I will return” was not a polite phrase—Paul really came back. How many of my promises to the Lord and to others were simply said and then left behind?
II. “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?”—Paul Asked About Life, Not Knowledge

Luke calls these men “disciples,” so outwardly they looked like believers: they believed in a Messiah, had repented, and had been baptized. But after speaking with them for a few moments, Paul sensed something was wrong. He did not quiz them on doctrine or rules; he asked one question that went straight to the core: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” What concerned Paul was not what they knew, but whether God was within them.

Their answer is heartbreaking: “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” It was not a refusal; they had simply never heard. They believed in a Messiah who was to come, but did not know that he had already come, died, risen, ascended, and poured out the Holy Spirit. Their faith had stopped short of Pentecost.

Of the three foundations of the 321 principles, “the Holy Spirit is my guide” is the one most easily overlooked. We can acknowledge with our minds that Jesus is our example; we can read with our eyes that Scripture is our standard; but the Spirit’s guidance has to be received with the heart. For someone who has never experienced the Holy Spirit, faith can only be propped up by one’s own strength—and however long one props it up, it remains only propping.
• Dare to ask yourself this question: not “How long have I believed?” but “When I believed, did the Holy Spirit come in?”
• Where did you stop? Is my faith lived after Pentecost, guided by the Spirit, or before Pentecost, waiting for a distant God?
III. “John baptized with the baptism of repentance”—Repentance That Stops at the Door

The baptism of John was not wrong; it was sent by God (John 1:33). Paul puts it fairly: “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.” John’s baptism had two parts: repentance, turning away from the old path; and pointing—believe in the one who comes after me.

Here is the problem: John’s baptism was a pointing finger, but these twelve men had stopped at the finger and had not followed it to see Jesus. They had repented but not believed; they stood at the door but had not gone in.

It is like a man who walks into a station holding a ticket. He has learned the signs on the platform and memorized the timetable, but he never boards the train. The signs are right, but the signs are not the destination.

Many people’s faith also stops here: they know they are sinners and have changed a few habits, but the center of their life has never changed masters. If repentance is only “leaving” and not “entering,” a person is left standing on an empty lot—the old is gone, the new has not come, and self steps back into the middle to reign once again.
• Repentance needs a destination: leaving sin is only turning around; after turning, we must walk toward Jesus.
• Do not stop at the finger: John, preachers, books, experiences—all are pointing fingers. Have I followed them to see him?
IV. “Baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus… the Holy Spirit came on them”—Change the Focus, and Everything Changes

Paul did not teach a new method; he did just one thing: he turned their focus from John to Jesus. As soon as they heard “that is, Jesus,” they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus; after their baptism Paul laid hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came upon them. Speaking in tongues and prophesying were the outward confirmation that the Spirit had come, just as on the day of Pentecost.

Some treat this passage as a formula, assuming that receiving the Spirit requires fixed steps. But throughout the book of Acts the Spirit’s coming is not uniform: in Jerusalem he came while the disciples waited and prayed (chapter 2); in Samaria he came when the apostles laid on hands (chapter 8); in Cornelius’s house he came before the sermon was even finished (chapter 10). What Luke wants to show is not a “method” but a “range”—each time the gospel crosses into a new realm, God himself confirms it: this place is mine too.

So the point is not the laying on of hands, nor tongues, but the name. John’s name could not bring down the Spirit, and neither could Paul’s; only “the name of the Lord Jesus” can. This is exactly what “let Jesus be King” looks like at the entrance of faith: not believing one more thing, but changing the center to him.
• Focus on Jesus: not the preacher, not the method, not the experience, but the one “who would come after him, that is, Jesus.”
• Confirmation is God’s work: how and when the Spirit comes is God’s sovereign right; my part is to yield the throne.
V. “In all there were about twelve men”—A Small Number, a Great Beginning

Three thousand at Pentecost, then five thousand, and now twelve. By human reckoning this is nothing, yet these twelve were the beginning of the church in Ephesus. In the next two years “all who lived in Asia… heard the word of the Lord” (19:10); the churches of Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis all went out from Ephesus; and the seven churches of Revelation were all in this land.

The Lord began his kingdom with twelve disciples, and now he begins the revival of Asia with twelve men. Building God’s system has never started with a grand scene, but with a small group who truly let Jesus be King; the realm grows out of people, not out of size.
• Do not despise small numbers: the Lord looks at “whether the Spirit is there,” not “how many there are.”
• Start with me: revival in Ephesus began with twelve; revival in my place can begin with just one—me.
321 Principles Insight: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide, Not My Knowledge

What is most startling in this passage is that “disciples” and “never heard that there is a Holy Spirit” can sit side by side. A person can be called a disciple and yet have no share in the Spirit; can be devout and yet stop at the door.

The old self, living for itself, is best at turning faith into something it can control: knowledge can be accumulated, habits can be formed, status can be obtained—all of it in “my” hands. The Holy Spirit is different: he cannot be managed, only obeyed; he is not a part of my faith—he comes to be Lord. One who has only the baptism of John is still king of his own life, just a little more moral.

What Paul did in Ephesus was not to add something, but to change the focus: from the pointing finger to the one pointed to. Once the focus changed, the Holy Spirit came. Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the mind—John’s baptism reached only the head, but the name of Jesus enters the heart.
a: Keep your promises
Paul said “I will return,” and he really did; what I say to the Lord and to others, I must follow through.
Ask honestly
Not “How long have I believed?” but “When I believed, did the Holy Spirit come in?”
Repentance needs a destination
Leaving sin is only turning around; after turning, walk toward Jesus, and do not stop on an empty lot reigning as my own king.
Change the focus, not the method
Not the preacher, the method or the experience, but the name of the Lord Jesus; make him the center and he will confirm the rest.
Begin small
Ephesus began with twelve; revival in my place can begin with me alone.
q: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” If Paul asked you this question face to face today, what would you answer? Is your faith lived before Pentecost, or after?

In your faith, is there a “pointing finger”—a preacher, a book, an experience—on which you have stayed too long, so that you have not truly walked toward Jesus? Are you willing to follow it until you see him?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that Paul returned to Ephesus as he had promised, and thank you for preparing there twelve men waiting to have their gap filled. We admit that we are often like them: we know we should repent but stop at the door; we carry the title of disciple but have not let the Holy Spirit rule our hearts.
Lord Jesus, today once again turn our focus from every pointing finger to you yourself. We do not want a faith that reaches only the head; we want your Spirit to dwell in our hearts as our guide for a lifetime. Remove from us the old self that is used to propping itself up and calculating with its own mind, and teach us to rely on the Spirit with our hearts; and use us, ordinary people that we are, like the twelve in Ephesus, to be the starting point of your revival in this land. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: He entered into the synagogue and spoke boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning God’s Kingdom.
But when some were hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.
God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul,
so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out.
But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, took on themselves to invoke over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.”
There were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this.
The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?”
The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Many also of those who had believed came, confessing, and declaring their deeds.
Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.
b: In the last devotion, the twelve men in Ephesus turned from the baptism of John to the name of the Lord Jesus, and the Holy Spirit came upon them. The revival of a whole city began with these twelve.

In this devotion, Luke condenses three years of ministry in Ephesus into thirteen verses: the synagogue, the school, handkerchiefs and aprons, seven false exorcists, and a heap of burned books of magic. One scene is more dramatic than the next, yet what Luke really wants us to see is a single sentence—“the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.”
I. “For three months… for two years”—From the Synagogue to the School

Paul went first to the synagogue as usual and “spoke boldly for a period of three months”—the longest he ever stayed in a synagogue. Later, “when some were hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude,” Paul left, “separated the disciples,” and moved into the school of Tyrannus.

The school of Tyrannus was a public lecture hall belonging to a teacher or owner named Tyrannus. Some ancient manuscripts add that Paul used it “from the fifth hour to the tenth”—from eleven in the morning to four in the afternoon. That was the hottest time of day in a Mediterranean city, when everyone went home to rest, the hall stood empty, and the rent was cheap. Paul worked at leather in the morning (20:34), and at midday, while others napped, he “reasoned daily” in the hall.

So it went for two years. The result: “all they who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord.” Paul himself did not travel through all of Asia; Ephesus, a meeting point of trade routes, turned the people passing through into seeds. The churches of Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis all grew out of the school during these two years (Col. 1:7; 4:13).
• Begin where you can find a place: a classroom left empty during others’ midday rest can become the gospel center of Asia.
• Daily: revival is not a big meeting but two years of “every day.”
II. “God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul”—Handkerchiefs and Aprons

“Special” in the original means “not of the ordinary kind,” and Luke himself admits it was unusual. The “handkerchiefs” were cloths for wiping sweat, and the “aprons” were what craftsmen tied on while working—neither was a religious object, but Paul’s leatherworking clothes. What God used was not a sacred relic but a cloth that had touched the sweat of a working man.

Notice the subject: “God worked… by the hands of Paul.” It was not that Paul’s hands had power, but that God worked through them; not that the handkerchiefs had power, but that God was willing. Ephesus was a superstitious city where people were used to believing that objects held magical power, so God spoke at a level they could understand—yet the message was not “Paul is great,” but “the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified.”
• The subject of power is God: whatever fruit there is in my service, the subject is always “God working through.”
• Work clothes can be used too: there is no need to wait for a religious occasion to serve; sweat and cloth at work are also in God’s hands.
III. “But who are you?”—A Borrowed Name Has No Authority

Verses 13–16 are the most dramatic scene in this passage. “Some of the wandering Jews, exorcists”—in the Mediterranean world of that time, Jewish exorcists were well known, since they held “the unspeakable name.” They saw that Paul’s casting out of spirits in the name of Jesus was effective, so they added the name to their own incantations: “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches!” Luke adds that those who did this were “seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest”—men with status, family and profession.

The evil spirit’s answer is strikingly precise: “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” The original uses two different words for “know”: for Jesus it means “recognize, acknowledge,” for Paul it means “know about, have heard of”; for these seven men, just “who are you?” Then the man with the evil spirit leaped on them, and the seven, beaten by two fists, fled naked and wounded from the house.

It is like someone who steals another person’s access card. The card is genuine and the door recognizes the card, but the guard behind the door looks up and says: you are not the owner of the card. A name can be borrowed, but authority cannot. Authority lies not in the pronunciation of the word “Jesus” but in a person’s relationship with Jesus.

The sons of Sceva are the most naked picture of self-centered service: wanting power but not the Lord; wanting results but not relationship; wanting to use the name of Jesus but refusing to let Jesus be King—trading spiritual language and technique for what they want. The demons are not afraid of such people.
• Demons recognize relationship, not jargon: when I open my mouth to pray, is what is between him and me real, or borrowed?
• To want power, first want the Lord: one who will not let Jesus be King will not have the authority of Jesus.
IV. “The name of the Lord Jesus was magnified”—After Fear, Exaltation

A farce, and yet the result was that the Lord’s name was magnified. The people of Ephesus saw clearly: the name of Jesus is not a spell to be used but the name of a living Lord; he knows who are his and who are not. Such fear is healthy—it restores Jesus from “a useful thing” to “the Lord to be revered.” This is exactly what it means to let Jesus receive all the glory: Paul did not even appear, yet even the evil spirit bore witness and gave glory to that name.
• Let him be restored as Lord: Jesus is not my tool; he is the King I must revere.
• Glory to the name: even demons recognize that name, so I must all the more not shift his glory onto myself.
V. “Brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all”—Repentance Worth Fifty Thousand

Note that verse 18 speaks of “those who had believed.” People who had already believed in the Lord still had books of magic at home. Ephesus was famous for sorcery, and the “Ephesian writings” were a widely used collection of spells; an Ephesian who came to faith may well have turned to the Lord in his reason while keeping a book in the drawer “just in case.” The incident of Sceva’s sons made them see that the name cannot be mixed with anything else. So they “confessed”—publicly admitting their sin; and then they “brought their books together and burned them”—not sold, but burned.

“Fifty thousand pieces of silver.” One piece was a laborer’s wage for a day; fifty thousand pieces was what a laborer would take well over a hundred years to earn. They could have sold the books and given the money, but they chose to burn them—because some things cannot be allowed to pass into other hands and can only be ended.

Self-denial here is not abstract: it is a person taking out of the drawer the book he cannot bear to part with and burning it in public. Our “books of magic” today may be a dependence or a habit—anything I still keep “just in case” after coming to the Lord. Luke closes with one sentence: “So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.” The word grows not through miracles, but through a group of people truly letting go of what is in their hands.
• The one in the drawer: after coming to faith, what do I still keep “just in case”?
• Burn, not sell: some things cannot change hands and can only be ended.
321 Principles Insight: A Name Can Be Borrowed, but a King Cannot

Ephesus was a city of names: the name of Artemis, the name of Sceva, hundreds of names in the spells. Yet from beginning to end in this passage, only one name truly has authority—the name of the Lord Jesus. That name cannot be borrowed; it can only be obeyed.

The self-centered person wants God’s power but not God as King; wants the results his name brings but not the lordship his name carries. But what demons recognize is not pronunciation but relationship. “But who are you?”—this question still asks us today: do I speak by virtue of my relationship with him, or by learned phrases and technique?

Paul’s handkerchiefs had power because “God worked through them”; Sceva’s sons had none because of “who are you?” The same name: on one side exalted, on the other humiliated, and the difference lies only in whether the person under that name has let him be King. When a group of believers is willing to burn fifty thousand pieces of silver worth of magic books, that is what letting Jesus be King looks like—and at that moment, “the word of the Lord grows and becomes mighty.”
a: Daily in the school
Revival is not one big meeting but two years of “every day”; begin where I can find a place.
The subject is God
The subject of any fruit in my service is always “God working through,” not my handkerchief.
Do not borrow the name
When I open my mouth to pray, first ask whether my relationship with him is real or borrowed.
Restore him as Lord
Jesus is not my tool but the King I must revere, and the glory is his alone.
Burn the book in the drawer
Whatever I still keep “just in case” after coming to faith, bring out and end it today.
q: The evil spirit asked, “But who are you?” When you pray or serve in the Lord’s name today, is your relationship with him one of real obedience, or of learned phrases?

The believers in Ephesus still kept books of magic at home after they believed. Is there something in your life you keep “just in case”? What is it worth? Are you willing to burn it rather than sell it?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that in Ephesus, a city full of names, you let us see that only the name of the Lord Jesus has real authority. Thank you for working miracles through Paul’s sweat-stained handkerchiefs, and thank you that through the humiliation of the sons of Sceva you made the people fear and magnified the name of your Son.
Lord Jesus, we admit that we too often want to borrow your name without letting you be King; we want your power but not your lordship. Search us, and make our relationship with you real and not borrowed. Shine also into the drawers of our hearts—those dependences, habits and things we still keep “just in case” after coming to faith—and give us courage to end them today. May your word grow and become mighty among us, and may all the glory go to your name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: Now after these things had ended, Paul determined in the Spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
Having sent into Macedonia two of those who served him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen,
whom he gathered together, with the workmen of like occupation, and said, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth.
You see and hear that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods that are made with hands.

Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”
b: In the last devotion, the believers in Ephesus piled up fifty thousand pieces of silver worth of magic books and burned them before everyone, and “the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.” The spiritual foundation of a whole city had been shaken.

But once a foundation is shaken, those who live off that foundation come forward to speak. Luke uses the phrase “after these things were accomplished” as a turning point: on one side Paul’s heart looks toward Rome; on the other the silversmith Demetrius looks at his own account book. Both men are “resolving,” one for the kingdom of God, the other for his own business. This passage unfolds in the contrast between these two minds.
I. “Paul purposed in the spirit”—Rome on His Map

In verse 21, “Paul purposed in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem.” “Purposed in the spirit” can mean Paul’s own resolve, or it can mean guidance in the Holy Spirit—Luke probably deliberately lets both meanings stand together: Paul’s plan was formed in the Spirit.

The plan had three stops. First Macedonia and Achaia—that is, back to Philippi, Thessalonica and Corinth—to collect the offerings from the churches for the poor saints in Jerusalem (1 Cor. 16:1–4); then up to Jerusalem to hand the love of the Gentile churches to the Jewish brothers with his own hands; and finally—“After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”

The word “must” is often a mark of God’s will in Luke’s writing: the Son of Man “must” suffer, “must” rise. When Paul says “I must see Rome,” he is convinced that Rome is in God’s plan; and the letter to the Romans he later wrote from Corinth says, “I long to see you” (Rom. 1:11). God’s servant has plans, but the plans are set in the Spirit; the way he would eventually reach Rome—in chains—was entirely unexpected, yet the “must” was still fulfilled. In verse 22 he first sent Timothy and Erastus to Macedonia; Erastus may be the city treasurer of Corinth (Rom. 16:23), a man of standing willing to lay down his post to run errands.
• Purpose in the Spirit: when I make plans, do I first calculate with my mind, or first become quiet in the Holy Spirit?
• Leave the “must” to God: the destination is his; the route and the way are his to arrange, and I only need to follow.
II. “No small disturbance about the Way”—Whose Interests the Gospel Touched

From chapter 9 on, Luke has called the Christian faith “the Way”—not a set of opinions but a road. Three years after this road entered Ephesus, some people began to be unable to bear it. Verse 24 introduces the main figure: Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis. The Artemis of Ephesus is not the bow-bearing moon goddess of Greek myth but the ancient fertility goddess of Asia Minor, pictured as a dark stone figure hung with fruit on her chest; her temple was about 130 meters long with 127 columns, one of the largest buildings in the world at that time, and the bank and refuge of all Asia. Every spring at the festival of Artemis, tens of thousands of pilgrims poured into Ephesus, and each one took a small silver shrine home—a whole industry chain.

Demetrius was the head of this chain. “Brought no little business to the craftsmen”—he earned not only for himself but for a whole group of people. So the source of the disturbance was not theology but economics: as the gospel prospered, orders for silver shrines dwindled.
• The Way will disturb: when the true gospel enters a place, it always meets someone’s interests; so it is in my own life.
• Discern the source of opposition: some opposition looks like it is for the faith, but is actually for business.
III. “By this business we have our wealth”—The Most Honest Sentence

In verses 25 and 26, Demetrius calls his fellow craftsmen together, and his opening words are strikingly frank: “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth.” He did not begin with the goddess; he began with money.

Then he quotes Paul: “They are no gods, that are made with hands.” That is exactly what Paul said in Athens (17:29), and Demetrius quotes it accurately—he understood the gospel and saw what it meant for him. He admits that Paul had swayed people “almost throughout all Asia.” An opponent ended up giving the fullest testimony to the gospel: two years in the school had indeed made all Asia hear.

Notice the order in Demetrius’s words: first “our business,” then “the temple of Artemis,” and only last “the majesty of the great goddess.” A person’s real order of priorities is often exposed at his most agitated moment. The first thing he cared about was getting rich; the goddess was only a reason placed behind it.
This is a mirror to hold up to ourselves. When I am agitated and opposed to something, are the reasons I give with my mouth and the reasons in my heart the same?
• Listen to your own first sentence: what comes out first when agitated is often the real number one in the heart.
• The opponent’s testimony: Demetrius admits the gospel has changed Asia—even enemies cannot deny his work.
IV. “The majesty of the great goddess would be destroyed”—Packaging Self-Interest as Piety

In verse 27, Demetrius brings his words to the highest level: business, the temple, the majesty of the goddess whom all the world worships. He is clever. If he had said only “we can’t make money,” his colleagues would have sympathized but the crowd would not have taken to the streets; so he translated the loss of business into the loss of the goddess, the loss of the city, the loss of the whole world. Once self-interest puts on the cloak of piety, it has the power to mobilize a whole city—in the next devotion we will see that these words really did set the whole city ablaze.

This is a trick the old self is best at: finding a sacred name for its own interests. What I will not let go of, I call “principle”; the person I will not forgive, I call “justice”; the position I will not give up, I call “the ministry.” The more spiritual the words, the deeper the self hides. Demetrius’s problem was not that he loved money—that would at least be honest; it was that he packaged love of money as love of the goddess.

It is like an old shop hanging out a sign reading “protecting tradition” to oppose a new shop down the street: the sign says culture, but the heart is thinking of revenue. There is nothing wrong with the sign; the wrong is using the sign to cover the account book. Pride is leaving one’s place and wanting to replace God; when I use God’s name to defend my own interests, I have already put God beneath me and made him serve me. Humility is returning to one’s place—letting God be God, and letting my account book be just an account book.
• Tear off the sacred label: what I protect with “spiritual reasons”—is any of it actually “my business”?
• Let God be God: God is not the guarantor of my interests; he is Lord, and I am the one who must obey.
321 Principles Insight: Resolved for God’s Kingdom, or for My Own Business

In these seven verses there are two men who “resolve in their hearts.” Paul resolves in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem and Rome, placing everything in God’s kingdom; Demetrius resolves before his account book, calling his colleagues together and placing everything in his own business. The former’s vision looks farther and farther; the latter’s grows narrower and narrower.

What is most sobering about Demetrius’s words is that they sound so pious. “The majesty of the great goddess”—how grand; yet his first sentence already gave his heart away: “By this business we have our wealth.” A self-centered life is not necessarily irreligious; it simply uses religion for its own purposes. Letting Jesus receive all the glory and using Jesus’ name to glorify oneself can look exactly alike on the outside; the difference lies only in who is truly first in the heart.

So we must keep returning to the most honest question: when I am agitated about something, what is the first thing that comes out of my mouth? If it is “mine,” then self is speaking; if it is “his,” then Jesus is King. From a human viewpoint to God’s viewpoint, from my own business to God’s kingdom—change the concept, and the life changes.
a: Purpose in the Spirit
Before making plans, become quiet in the Holy Spirit; the destination is his, the route his to arrange.
Accept the disturbance of the Way
When the gospel enters my life, it will surely touch some of my interests; when it does, it is time to let go.
Hear your first sentence
What comes out first when I am agitated is the real number one in my heart.
Tear off the sacred label
What I protect with spiritual reasons—ask honestly whether it is “my business.”
Let God be God
No longer use his name to serve me, but return to my place and let him be Lord.
q: Think of the last time you were agitated in opposing or insisting on something. What was the first reason you gave? Was it the same as the real reason in your heart?
Paul “purposed in the spirit”; Demetrius “resolved before his account book.” Where is a decision you are making now being settled? If you placed it back into God’s kingdom, would it look different?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that Paul purposed in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem and Rome, with his eyes on your kingdom; and thank you for honestly recording Demetrius, that we might see how people package their own business as piety.
Lord Jesus, search our hearts. We admit that we too are often like Demetrius: with our mouths we speak of your glory, but in our hearts we think of our own loss; we protect with spiritual reasons what we will not let go, and use your name to serve ourselves. Tear off from us every sacred label, and let us hear the real voice of our hearts first when we are agitated, and then repent before you. Make us, like Paul, purpose in the Spirit, place our plans in your hands, let you be God, and let us return to our place as human beings. May everything we do be for your kingdom and not for our own business; may you receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When they heard this they were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel.
When Paul wanted to enter in to the people, the disciples didn’t allow him.
Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and begged him not to venture into the theater.
Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of them didn’t know why they had come together.
They brought Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people.
But when they perceived that he was a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

When the town clerk had quieted the multitude, he said, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who doesn’t know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus?
Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet and to do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess.
If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them press charges against one another.
But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in the regular assembly.
For indeed we are in danger of being accused concerning today’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.”
When he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.
b: In the last devotion, the silversmith Demetrius packaged his business loss as “the majesty of the great goddess will be destroyed.” Once self-interest puts on the cloak of piety, it has the power to mobilize a whole city.

In this devotion, those words really set the city ablaze. Luke writes the riot most vividly and most ironically: the whole city in uproar, yet “the majority did not know why they had come together”; slogans shouted to the skies, and in the end a city official sent the people home with a few words. God’s servant barely appears in this storm, yet God’s hand is there from beginning to end.
I. “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”—Two Hours of Slogans

When the silversmiths heard Demetrius, they “were filled with anger” and began to shout; “the whole city was filled with confusion.” “Confusion” in the original is the word for chaos, and “some therefore cried one thing, and some another” in verse 32 uses the same word. This was a city that had lost its order.

The crowd could not catch Paul, so they seized two of his companions: Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians. Aristarchus was from Thessalonica and later went with Paul all the way to Rome (27:2); Paul called him from prison “my fellow prisoner” (Col. 4:10). The two men were dragged into the theater—the largest public place in Ephesus, seating more than twenty thousand.

Then comes verse 34: twenty thousand people, two hours, one slogan. The nature of a slogan is that it requires no thinking, only shouting along; and the longer people shout, the less they know what they are shouting.
• A slogan is not truth: a loud voice, many people and a long time cannot make a sentence true.
• Am I shouting along? In the emotions of a crowd, do I discern with my heart, or echo with my throat?
II. “The disciples wouldn’t allow him”—Even the Brave Must Be Willing to Be Counseled

Paul was brave. When his companions were seized, his first reaction was to rush in and stand before twenty thousand roaring people to speak for them. This was his usual way—stoned at Lystra, he went back into the city the next day. But this time the disciples would not allow it, and “certain also of the Asiarchs” sent to urge him.

“Asiarchs” were among the highest-ranking men of the province of Asia, who presided over provincial festivals and came from the wealthiest families. Luke says they were “his friends”—a Jew preaching the gospel had become a friend of the leading figures of the province. This shows that Paul was no agitator, as even the officials knew; and the gospel did not spread by confrontation but through relationships.

Paul listened. He did not insist on his own courage; he submitted to his brothers’ restraint. The hardest lesson for the brave is often not charging ahead but being willing to stop when others hold them back. Humility looks very concrete here: a man with every reason to rush in, because his brothers said “no,” stayed where he was.
• Being counseled is also obedience: God’s guidance sometimes comes to me through a brother’s “don’t.”
• Courage needs the ability to stop: charging ahead is easy; being willing to stop when held back is true self-denial.
III. “The majority did not know why they had come together”—A Crowd Has Only a Voice, No Mind

Verse 32 is the most ironic sentence in the passage: “the majority did not know why they had come together.” Then the Jews pushed forward a man named Alexander, wanting to distance themselves before the crowd: this matter had nothing to do with the Jews. Alexander “motioned with his hand”—raising his hand for silence to speak—but as soon as the crowd recognized he was a Jew (and Jews did not worship idols either), they did not care what he wanted to say and took up the slogan again, for two hours straight.

This is what a crowd is like: it does not need to know why, only for someone to start; it does not need to hear what you say, only to recognize “which side” you are on. Today we do not need to enter a theater; every day there are such theaters on our phones—one sentence forwarded, and tens of thousands shout along.

Within a crowd, people stop using even their minds, and only emotion is left. A person who lets Jesus be King, when the crowd is shouting, will first stop and ask: Do I know why this is happening? Have I heard the other side speak? When the focus is on Jesus, we will not be carried along by the noise.
• Ask why first: before shouting along, ask yourself whether you know how things came about.
• Don’t judge people by “side”: Alexander was rejected before he opened his mouth; do I too often judge people by labels?
IV. “The town clerk had quieted the multitude”—God Used a Civil Servant to Stop the Storm

In verse 35 a figure appears whom Luke calls simply “the town clerk.” He was the chief administrator of the city council of Ephesus and the liaison between the city and the Roman governor—in today’s terms, mayor and secretary-general in one.

His words have four layers. First, he took the crowd’s side: who does not know that Ephesus is the guardian of the temple of Artemis and of “the image which fell down from Zeus” (perhaps a meteorite)? “Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet”—meaning, if the goddess is really so great, why must you shout for her? Second, he spoke fairly for Gaius and Aristarchus: “They are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of our goddess.” After three years of Paul’s preaching, even the officials testified that he had not insulted the idols—he preached Christ and did not curse others. Third, he pointed to the proper channels: there were courts, there were proconsuls, there was the lawful assembly of citizens, to be “settled in the regular assembly.” Fourth, he named the real danger: “We are in danger of being accused concerning today’s riot, there being no cause.” What Rome could least tolerate was rioting, and a city called to account for it might lose its self-government.

An unbelieving civil servant said what Paul wanted to say but could not. God does not need his servant to appear in order to calm a storm; he can use someone concerned only with the order of the city to bring about the safety of his servant. However chaotic the circumstances, he is still the one who reigns.
• God’s hand is where people cannot see: he can use anyone to stop a storm, including unbelievers.
• One can preach without cursing idols: even the clerk testified that Paul did not blaspheme the goddess; can my way of sharing the gospel stand such scrutiny?
V. “He dismissed the assembly”—The Shouting Disperses, the Word Remains

The two hours of slogans simply dispersed. This verse contrasts sharply with verse 20: “So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty”—“he dismissed the assembly.” On one side the word spreads wider and wider; on the other, a noise that scatters once the shouting is done. Today the temple of Artemis has only a single column standing in a marsh, while the church in Ephesus became the first of the seven churches of Asia.
The self-centered rely on noise to hold up a scene, and when the noise stops nothing is left; the self-denying stand on the word, and when the storm passes, the word remains.
• Discern what will scatter and what will remain: noise scatters, the word remains; on which am I building my life?
• Carry on after the storm: what Paul did next was to “call the disciples to himself and exhort them” (20:1).
321 Principles Insight: The Focus Is on Jesus, Not the Circumstances

In this passage Paul does almost nothing—he wanted to go in and was held back; his companions were seized and he stayed outside; the one who spoke for him was an unbelieving clerk. From a human viewpoint it was the most helpless day; from God’s viewpoint it was the day God himself reigned.

The old self, living for itself, must “do something” in a storm—rush in, argue, prove itself. But this time God held Paul back through his brothers’ “don’t,” and then calmed everything in his own way. Sometimes letting Jesus be King does not look like stepping forward but like being willing to stay where you are and watch what he does.
