In these ten verses the circumstances reach their worst: misunderstanding, riot, beating, chains, shouts to kill. Paul had done everything right—he obeyed the elders, performed the rite of purification, entered the temple out of love—and in return got all this. If the focus were on circumstances, this would be a complete failure.

But Luke’s pen keeps reminding us of another pair of hands: someone brought the news, the officer ran down immediately, the chains were put on, the man was carried. Every seemingly bad action was moving Paul from the edge of death into the barracks. The road that would take him to Rome began from these very steps.

In such circumstances a self-centered life asks: Why me? I clearly did right. A self-denying life asks: Lord, what are you doing here? The former looks at circumstances and grows ever more troubled; the latter looks at Jesus and sees him fulfilling, through a Gentile officer, what he had long said. The focus on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances—this is not a word of comfort but the only place to stand in chaos. Rely on the Spirit with the heart and you will see those hands; rely on yourself with the mind and you will see only chains.
a: Don’t turn “supposed” into “this is so”
Before forwarding or discussing, confirm whether I have seen the whole.
The door closed, the road did not
The door people shut is not God’s only door.
Recognize protection’s shape
The chains that make me unfree may be the very way the Lord shields me.
Don’t shout along
When the crowd is loudest, first ask whether I know the truth.
Let yourself be carried
When misunderstood, don’t rush to prove myself; like the Lord, place myself in the Father’s hands.
q: Think of the last time you relayed, forwarded or discussed something: was what you said what you saw yourself, or what you “supposed”? If you were the other person, how would you want others to act?
Is there now in your life a “chain”—something that makes you unfree and you do not understand why? Try changing the question: not “Why me?” but “Lord, what are you doing here?”
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for honestly recording this riot, so that we see a person can do every single thing right and still be misunderstood and bound. Thank you also that in the most chaotic scene you had already arranged the one who brought the news, the officer who ran down, and the chains that saved his life.
Lord, we admit that we are often the ones who turn “supposed” into “this is so,” and often the ones who shout along with the crowd; and when we ourselves are misunderstood we hurry to prove ourselves and look at circumstances until our hearts are full of trouble. Turn our focus from circumstances back to you, that even in chains we may recognize your hand. Give us Paul’s quietness, not struggling when carried and not defending when shouted at, only placing ourselves in your hands; for you walked this road before, and you know where it leads. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he asked the commanding officer, “May I speak to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek?
Aren’t you then the Egyptian, who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?”
But Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”
When he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the stairs, beckoned with his hand to the people. When there was a great silence, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, saying,
b: In the last devotion, Paul was misunderstood in the temple, beaten and bound in iron chains, and the soldiers carried him up the steps of the barracks while the crowd behind shouted, “Away with him!”

These four short verses are a crack in the door between riot and sermon. A man who had just been beaten, his hands chained, opened his mouth to say one sentence in the last moment before being carried into the barracks. That one sentence turned a riot that was nearly over into a testimony to all Jerusalem. These four verses show us that a person who has denied self, at his most bedraggled, remains clear-headed, courteous, and knows who he is.
I. “May I speak to you?”—Composure in Disarray

In verse 37, “as Paul was about to be brought into the barracks”—the door of the barracks was right in front of him, and once inside the chance to speak would be gone. At this last step Paul opened his mouth: “May I speak to you?”

Look at the tone of this sentence. He had just been beaten, his clothes perhaps torn, blood on him, his hands chained, the crowd behind shouting to kill him. When such a man speaks, we would expect him to cry out against injustice, to plead for help, to protest. But what Paul says is an extremely courteous request: may I? The original is “Is it permitted for me to say something to you?”—a polite question.

This composure was not natural temperament but the result of who reigned within him. If the focus is on self, when beaten there is only anger and fear; if the focus is on Jesus, a person can still see the officer in front of him, still remember courtesy, still think of the opportunity for the gospel. Paul sang hymns in the prison at Philippi (16:25) and here asks politely—the same man, the same source.
• Composure has a source: to remain courteous in disarray is because there is within a King who is not in disarray.
• Speak even at the last step: the chance often has room for only one sentence, and the self-denying do not use it to cry out against injustice.
II. “Aren’t you the Egyptian?”—Mistaken Again

In verses 37 and 38, the commanding officer heard Paul speaking Greek and was astonished: “Do you know Greek?” He had already assigned Paul an identity in his mind: “Aren’t you the Egyptian, who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?”

The historian Josephus records that a few years earlier an Egyptian who called himself a prophet led a large crowd up the Mount of Olives, claiming the walls of the city would fall at his command; the governor Felix sent troops to suppress them, killing hundreds, but the Egyptian escaped. “Assassins” in the original is “dagger men,” a group of killers who stabbed pro-Roman figures in crowds. The officer thought that the man who had caused the whole city to riot was the escaped Egyptian come back.

This was the second time in one short day that Paul was mistaken for someone else. The Jews from Asia supposed he had brought Gentiles into the temple; the Roman officer supposed he was the rebel leader from Egypt. One side said he betrayed the Jews, the other that he rebelled against Rome—both wrong, both certain.

We too are often “supposed” in this way: given a label, and then people treat us according to the label. At such a time “self” has two reactions: one is rage—how dare you see me that way; the other is self-pity—no one understands me anyway. Paul had neither; he simply explained calmly.
• A label is not me: the identity others assign me needs no emotional reply, only a factual explanation.
• No need to panic when both sides are wrong: truth does not depend on others’ views; who I am, the Lord knows.
III. “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city”—Knowing Who You Are
In verse 39, Paul’s answer is only three sentences: I am a Jew; from Tarsus in Cilicia; a citizen of no insignificant city. Then a request: “Please allow me to speak to the people.”

Tarsus was a famous city in the eastern Roman Empire, on the southern coast of present-day Turkey, with a renowned school and many philosophers, ranking with Athens and Alexandria, and was a free city whose residents enjoyed privileges. “No insignificant city” was a common expression of the time; when Paul said it, it was not boasting but explaining to a Roman officer: I am not a desperate outlaw from the wilderness; I am a person with a background that can be verified.

There is an important distinction here. Humility is not self-belittling, not describing oneself as worthless; humility is returning to one’s place—letting God be God and letting man be man. God caused Paul to be born in Tarsus and gave him learning, language, citizenship; all this was God’s arrangement, and Paul need not pretend he did not have it. He knew who he was and knew what it was all for: “Please allow me to speak to the people.” He mentioned his origins not to gain respect but to gain an opportunity to preach.

The proud use identity to lift themselves up; the self-belittling use identity to deny themselves; the self-denying use identity to serve the Lord. The three may have identical résumés; the difference lies only in whom the résumé points to.
• Know who I am: the birth, learning and abilities God gave me need not be denied; just ask whom they point to.
• Identity is a tool, not a throne: when I mention my background, is it to be respected, or for the Lord’s work?
IV. “He motioned with his hand to the people, and there was a great silence”—Speaking in Their Language

In verse 40, the officer permitted it. Paul “stood on the stairs”—the stone steps from the Antonia Fortress to the outer court of the temple, where the soldiers had just carried him up and which now became a platform. He “motioned with his hand to the people,” a familiar gesture (12:17, 13:16), and the crowd that had just been shouting “Away with him!” “made a great silence.”

Then Luke records a key detail: “he spoke to them in the Hebrew language.” To the officer he had spoken Greek; now to the crowd he switched to Hebrew—the everyday language of the Jews at the time, Aramaic. Verse 2 of the next chapter says that when they heard him speak in Hebrew, “they were even more quiet.”

It is like tuning a radio. The signal is always there, but unless you tune to the other person’s frequency, he hears only noise. Paul could use whichever language he wished, but he chose not what came most smoothly to himself but what the listeners could take in best. To the officer, the officer’s words; to the people, the people’s words—this is not pleasing people but love. The first act of love is to tune oneself to the other’s frequency.
The self-centered speak caring whether they speak well; the self-denying speak caring whether the other can take it in. The former’s focus is on self, the latter’s on the person.
• Tune to the other’s frequency: when I speak with family, colleagues, friends exploring faith, do I use words they can understand?
• Steps become a platform: the Lord can turn the most bedraggled place into the strongest witness stand.
321 Principles Insight: The Self-Denying Know Who They Are

These four verses hold three identities: the Egyptian rebel the officer supposed, the apostate the Jews supposed, and the Jew of Tarsus Paul himself named. The first two were pasted on by others, the third was given by God.

Self-denial is not having no identity, not wiping oneself out. Self-denial is not nothing but entering the limitless—Paul did not deny who he was; he handed all of who he was to the Lord, and so the learning of Tarsus, Greek, Hebrew, Roman citizenship, all became tools of the gospel. The self-centered hold identity in their hands to protect and lift themselves; the self-denying place identity in the Lord’s hands, to be used however he wishes.

Here is what letting Jesus be King concretely looks like: remaining courteous in chains, not angry when mistaken, mentioning one’s background only to gain an opportunity to preach, switching to the other’s language when opening one’s mouth. In all this the focus was not on Paul, so in his most bedraggled moment he was the clearest-headed person on the scene.
a: Courteous even in disarray
When wronged or chained, still see the person before me and still remember to say “may I?”
Don’t answer labels with emotion
However others “suppose” me, explain with facts, not with rage or self-pity.
Know who I am
The background and abilities God gave me need not be denied, only pointed to the Lord.
Identity used by the Lord
When mentioning my background, ask whether it is to be respected or for the Lord’s work.
Tune to the other’s frequency
Before speaking, think: is this what comes smoothest for me, or what he can take in best?
q: Think of the last time you were given a wrong label: was your first reaction rage, self-pity, or calm explanation? What does that reaction tell you about who was reigning in your heart at that time?
Is there someone near you to whom you have always spoken on “your own frequency” and who has never been able to take it in? Are you willing to say it differently for him today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us see Paul’s composure in chains. He had just been beaten, with people behind him shouting to remove him, yet he remained courteous, clear-headed, and thinking of the opportunity for the gospel. Thank you for letting us know that this composure was not his temperament but the result of your reigning within him.
Lord, we admit that when misunderstood we often have only anger or self-pity, that when we mention ourselves it is often to be respected, and that when we speak we often choose only what comes smoothly to us. Move our focus off ourselves, that even at our most bedraggled we can still see the person before us; make us know who we are, neither denying what you have given nor clinging to it, but placing each thing in your hands to be your tool. Give us also the ears and tongue of love, willing to tune first to the other’s frequency and, in words he understands, tell him about you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense which I now make to you.”
When they heard that he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, they were even more quiet. He said,

“I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God, even as you all are today.
I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.

As also the high priest and all the council of the elders testify, from whom also I received letters to the brothers, and traveled to Damascus to bring them also who were there to Jerusalem in bonds to be punished.
As I made my journey, and came close to Damascus, about noon, suddenly a great light shone around me from the sky.
I fell to the ground, and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute.’
“Those who were with me indeed saw the light and were afraid, but they didn’t understand the voice of him who spoke to me.
I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Arise, and go into Damascus. There you will be told about all things which are appointed for you to do.’
When I couldn’t see for the glory of that light, being led by the hand of those who were with me, I came into Damascus.
One Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived in Damascus,
came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight!’ In that very hour I looked up at him.
He said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth.
For you will be a witness for him to all men of what you have seen and heard.
Now why do you wait? Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.’
b: In the last devotion, Paul stood on the steps of the barracks and motioned to the people; the whole place fell silent, and he began in Hebrew.

This devotion is what he said on the steps. The crowd that had just been shouting “Away with him!” now quieted to listen. Paul did not give theology or argue the law; he told one thing: how he himself met Jesus. This is the second time Acts records the events on the Damascus road (the first is in chapter 9, the third in chapter 26); Luke records the same event three times, showing how important it is. And the way Paul tells his testimony sets an example for us: who is the main character of a testimony?
I. “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense which I now make to you”—First Stand Among Them

In verses 1 and 2, Paul’s opening: “Brothers and fathers, listen.” These were exactly the first words of Stephen before the council (7:2). “Defense” in the original is “apology,” but we will find that his defense is not a defense of himself; it introduces Jesus to them.

“When they heard that he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, they were even more quiet.” The moment the mother tongue is spoken, hostility is halved. Before giving any reasoning, Paul let them know: I am one of you.
• First stand among them: for a testimony to be heard, people must first feel you are not an outsider.
• The aim of the defense: not to prove I was not wrong but to introduce the Lord.
II. “Being zealous for God, even as you all are this day”—I Was Once You

In verses 3–5, Paul accounts for himself with three verbs: born in Tarsus, brought up in Jerusalem, taught at the feet of Gamaliel. Gamaliel was the most respected rabbi of the time (5:34); being his student was like being a student of the finest university today. “Instructed according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers,” and then a key sentence: “being zealous for God, even as you all are this day.”

This sentence carries great weight. Why did this crowd want to kill him today? Zeal for the law. Paul said: I understand; I was once even more zealous than you—I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women, as the high priest and all the elders could testify, and I even took letters to Damascus to arrest people.

He did not stand opposite them to accuse; he stood among them and said: I am you. This was not rhetoric but fact; precisely because it was fact, it had power. A person who was once like you telling you why he changed is far more powerful than someone who never understood you telling you that you are wrong.
• Don’t stand opposite: to those who do not yet believe, first admit that I was once like them, rather than first pointing out their mistakes.
• Zeal is not rightness: Paul’s zeal once took him to kill people; zeal itself is not the standard, Scripture is.
III. “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”—That Light and That Question

In verses 6–9, as he traveled, about noon—the noonday sun is already at its brightest, yet “a great light from heaven” shone brighter than the sun (26:13). He fell to the ground and heard a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

“Persecuting me.” What Saul persecuted was the church, “those of the Way,” yet the voice from heaven said: you are persecuting me. The Lord counts his people and himself as one—to hurt them is to hurt him. This was the starting point of Saul’s lifelong theology, and later he would write: the church is the body of Christ.

“Who are you, Lord?” This was the first question he asked. He called him “Lord” yet did not know who he was—the light had already told him he faced God, only he did not know who God turned out to be. The answer came: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.”
Notice that Paul used the title “the Nazarene” before the crowd—the name this crowd despised most (John 1:46). He did not avoid it, because it was exactly the name the one in heaven called himself.
• To hurt people is to hurt the Lord: every harsh word I say to brothers and sisters today the Lord counts as said to himself.
• “Who are you?” is the starting point: all real change begins with admitting that I did not know him.
IV. “What shall I do, Lord?” “Led by the hand by those who were with me”—The “Self” Fell
In verses 10 and 11, Paul’s second question: “What shall I do, Lord?”

This is a question that yields the throne. A few minutes earlier he held letters in his hand and decided who should be arrested; now he asks: what shall I do? The Lord did not tell him everything at once, saying only: “Arise, and go into Damascus. There you will be told about all things which are appointed for you to do.” First enter the city, then you will be told. Obedience first, understanding after.

The picture in verse 11 is even more moving: “When I couldn’t see for the glory of that light, being led by the hand by those who were with me, I came into Damascus.” That Saul, with his letters and his men, going to arrest people, was led by the hand like a child into the city.

This is what the old self’s falling looks like. Not that he became useless, but that the “self” that reigned over itself fell. From this moment he was no longer the man who “knows what to do” but the man who asks, “What shall I do, Lord?” The first act of self-denial is often to be led by the hand along a road one cannot see.
• Obedience first, understanding after: the Lord often first asks me to arise and enter the city, and tells me the next step once I am there.
• Let someone lead you by the hand: sometimes God asks me first to lose my sight, so that I learn to trust those he sends.
V. “Brother Saul” “Arise, be baptized, calling on his name”—Accepted, Sent, Washed

In verses 12–16, Ananias appears. Paul introduces him to this Jewish audience with special emphasis: “a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived there”—chapter 9 calls him a “disciple,” here he is called a devout man who kept the law. The same man; Paul chose to introduce the side most acceptable to his hearers.

The first words Ananias spoke were: “Brother Saul.” A man who days earlier had come to arrest him was called brother. This is the gospel—acceptance comes before the repentant one has made any restitution.

Then the sending: “The God of our fathers has appointed you”—not a new God but the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; “to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth,” and “you will be a witness for him to all men.” “All men,” in the original “all people”—a word that in the next devotion will detonate the whole crowd, because it includes the Gentiles.

Finally the washing: “Now why do you wait? Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name.” Before the crowd Paul openly confessed: I have sins, and my sins need washing away. A man blameless under the law at the feet of Gamaliel said he needed his sins washed away—and the way of washing was to call on the name of Jesus.
• Acceptance comes before restitution: the gospel first calls a man “brother,” then calls him to arise.
• Do not wait: once I know what to do, I arise; delay is the last struggle of “self.”
321 Principles Insight: The Main Character of a Testimony Is Jesus

This is a testimony. But notice how Paul tells it: he speaks of his past to show how the Lord turned him around; he speaks of the light, with the main character being the one who shines; he speaks of Ananias, with the point being what God said through him. From beginning to end Paul is present, yet not one sentence boasts of himself.

When looking at a group photo, the first glance always looks for oneself. Testimonies often become like this too—speaking of God’s works while the camera keeps pointing at oneself: how zealous I was, how much I sacrificed, how blessed I am. After such a testimony, people remember the speaker, not the Lord. What letting Jesus receive all the glory looks like in testimony is this: the camera points at him, and I am only the one knocked down by the light, led by the hand, called brother, and washed clean.

And “What shall I do, Lord?” is the shortest prayer of letting Jesus be King. The self-centered ask “What shall I do?”; the self-denying ask “What shall I do, Lord?” One word of difference decides who sits on the throne. Paul began asking this question on the Damascus road and asked it all his life, all the way to Rome.
a: First stand among them
To those who do not yet believe, first admit I was once like this, then tell how the Lord changed me.
Remember that hurting people is hurting the Lord
Every word to brothers and sisters is counted as said to the Lord himself.
Ask the right question
Change “What shall I do?” to “What shall I do, Lord?”
Be willing to be led by the hand
On a road I cannot see, trust those God sends.
Point the camera at the Lord
When giving a testimony, move the focus from my zeal and sacrifice back to the Lord who shines.
q: The last time you told someone your testimony, at whom was the camera pointed? If every “I” were taken out of that testimony, would what was left still be enough for people to know the Lord?
Is there something today that you already know the Lord wants you to do but you are still “waiting”? What exactly does “arise” mean for you in concrete action?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that on the road to Damascus you stopped a zealous man going in the wrong direction, struck him down with a light brighter than the sun, and led him into the city by another’s hand. Thank you for letting us see that you count your people and yourself as one, and that to hurt them is to hurt you.
Lord, we admit that our zeal is often not the standard and that the main character of our testimonies is often ourselves. Turn our camera back to you, that we may speak of our past only to show your grace, and not seize your light when we tell of your works. Teach us to ask every day, “What shall I do, Lord?” rather than deciding for ourselves what to do; and give us a heart willing to be led by the hand, trusting the people and the road you arrange when we cannot see ahead. May we wait no longer, but arise and call on your name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: “When I had returned to Jerusalem, and while I prayed in the temple, I fell into a trance,
and saw him saying to me, ‘Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive testimony concerning me from you.’
I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue those who believed in you.
When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I also was standing by, consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of those who killed him.’
“He said to me, ‘Depart, for I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles.’”
They listened to him until he said that; then they lifted up their voice and said, “Rid the earth of this fellow, for he isn’t fit to live!”
As they cried out, threw off their cloaks, and threw dust into the air,
the commanding officer commanded him to be brought into the barracks, ordering him to be examined by scourging, that he might know for what crime they shouted against him like that.
When they had tied him up with thongs, Paul asked the centurion who stood by, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?”
When the centurion heard it, he went to the commanding officer and told him, “Watch what you are about to do, for this man is a Roman!”
The commanding officer came and asked him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He said, “Yes.”
The commanding officer answered, “I bought my citizenship for a great price.” Paul said, “But I was born a Roman.”
Immediately those who were about to examine him departed from him, and the commanding officer also was afraid when he realized that he was a Roman, because he had bound him.
b: In the last devotion, Paul on the steps told how he met Jesus: the light, being led by the hand into the city, Ananias calling him “brother,” arising to be baptized and have his sins washed away. The crowd listened quietly all the while.

In this devotion, the testimony continues but suddenly breaks off on a single word. Then the whip is brought out, the straps are tied on, and Paul says one sentence that makes everyone in the barracks stop. These thirteen verses show us two things: where human pride explodes, and how a self-denying person uses his own identity.
I. “While I was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance”—The Lord Spoke to Him in the Temple

In verses 17 and 18, Paul goes on to speak of what happened after he believed. He returned to Jerusalem (9:26) and was “praying in the temple.” Note: the charge against him was defiling the temple, and what he says is, even after I believed I still went to the temple to pray, and the Lord appeared to me there. This is an answer to the accusation, and it is also fact.

“Fell into a trance” is in the original “in a vision”—the man was still in the temple, but his spirit was taken by the Lord to another level. The Lord said: “Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they won’t receive testimony concerning me from you.” These words sound especially true today—he was standing in Jerusalem giving testimony, and the people here were about to refuse it. The Lord had said so more than twenty years earlier.
• The one who prays hears: the Lord’s guidance often comes to those who are praying, not to those busy planning.
• The Lord said it long ago: the refusal I meet today the Lord already knew, and had already arranged another road for me.
II. “Lord, they themselves know that I…”—A Stretch of Arguing with the Lord

In verses 19 and 20, Paul’s reaction is very real: he argued with the Lord. He mentioned how he used to imprison and beat believers, and how, when Stephen was killed, he stood by approving. His logic was: Lord, I am most useful staying in Jerusalem. The people here all know how I once persecuted the church; seeing that I now believe, the most persuasive witness would be me.

This is a very spiritual argument, yet its core is still “I”—my experience, my persuasiveness, my usefulness. The Lord did not discuss it, but said one sentence: “Depart, for I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles.”

The best-hidden form of “self” is using “I am most useful” to resist the Lord’s sending. It looks like zeal but is really unwillingness to hand over the decision. The Lord’s plan is not built on who is most useful, but only on whom he wants to send.

Note also that Paul mentioned Stephen before the crowd and admitted he “stood by, approving.” This was the wound of his life, and he did not hide it. A person truly forgiven has no need to cover up the worst stretch of his life.
• “I’m most useful” is also self: the Lord’s sending does not depend on where I think I fit best.
• Don’t hide wounds: the forgiven can openly speak of the most unbearable stretch of their past.
III. “Go to the Gentiles”—One Word Detonates the Whole Place

In verses 21–23, the Lord said: “I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles.” When the crowd heard this sentence, they raised their voices: “Rid the earth of such a fellow, for he isn’t fit to live!” They threw off their clothes and flung dust into the air—actions of extreme rage.

Think about it: they had tolerated “Jesus of Nazareth,” tolerated the vision, the light from heaven, baptism to wash away sins, and none of it exploded. What exploded was the word “Gentiles.” Because that sentence amounts to saying: God has given the grace you alone held to those you despise too. What it touched was not their theology but their pride—the pride of being chosen.

It is like an airport VIP lounge. Frequent travelers enter by membership and feel it is their due. One day the airline announces that today everyone may come in. The angriest are not those outside but those inside—they lost nothing, only the superiority of “others don’t have it, I do.” Pride is leaving one’s place and wanting to replace God—deciding who is worthy of grace is exactly taking God’s place. When God blesses someone we think unworthy, is there a voice within us saying, “Away with him”?
• The point where pride detonates: what I can least bear is often not what I lose but that others also receive what I thought only I deserved.
• Grace has no VIP lounge: God’s grace is not for the worthy but for the unworthy, myself included.
IV. “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman and not found guilty?”—The Right Word at the Right Time

In verses 24–26, the commanding officer, who did not understand Hebrew and did not know why the crowd was so enraged, ordered Paul brought in and “examined by scourging.” The Roman scourge was leather straps studded with bone and metal; a beating could cripple a man for life or even kill him; this was the standard way to interrogate slaves and foreigners: beat first, until the truth is told.
“As they tied him up with the thongs,” just about to begin, Paul said to the centurion standing by: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?”

Roman law explicitly forbade binding or scourging a citizen without trial, on pain of severe penalty. Paul chose this moment to speak—not while the crowd was beating him, but when the Romans themselves were about to break the law. At Philippi he mentioned it only after he had been beaten (16:37); this time he mentioned it before the whip fell.

Why did he mention it? Not for revenge, and not to escape. Before the crowd he would rather be beaten than not give his testimony; in the barracks he used his citizenship to protect the body that could go on giving testimony, and also set a precedent for the later church: believing in Jesus is not breaking the law.
• Identity is for the Lord’s use: Paul’s citizenship, like his Tarsus learning, was a tool, to be used when it should be used.
• The right word at the right time: to endure when one should endure and speak when one should speak takes the Spirit’s guidance, not temper.
V. “I bought this citizenship for a great price” “But I was born a Roman”—Bought and Born

In verses 27–29, the officer came himself to ask: “Tell me, are you a Roman?” Paul said, “Yes.” The officer said something sincere: “I bought this citizenship for a great price.” His name was Claudius Lysias (23:26), a name suggesting he had bought citizenship during the reign of Emperor Claudius—at that time citizenship could be bought from palace officials at great cost. Paul answered: “But I was born a Roman.”

One paid money to buy it, the other had it from birth. The one who bought it always has a bit of uneasiness within; the one who was born with it never needs to prove it. This says something in the gospel exactly: our standing in God’s household is not bought with good works but comes from being born again (John 3:3). A bought identity makes one keep worrying “is it enough”; an inborn identity makes one secure.
So those who were about to examine him left, and the officer “was afraid”—binding a Roman citizen was itself a crime.
• Identity is not bought: my place in God’s household was gained by new birth and does not need to be exchanged for performance.
• Security comes from birth: knowing whose child I am, I need not prove myself at every interrogation.
321 Principles Insight: The Detonation Point of Pride, and the Identity of the Self-Denying

This passage holds two attitudes toward identity. The crowd clutched the identity of “the chosen,” and on hearing that Gentiles too received grace they wanted to kill; Paul held the identity of “Roman citizen” but took it out only when it should be used, to preserve the opportunity to keep giving testimony. The same sort of identity: one became the detonation point of pride, the other a tool of service. The difference is whether the identity is clutched in one’s own hand or placed in the Lord’s. The self-centered clutch identity and use it to draw lines between who is worthy and who is not; the self-denying lay identity down, to be used when the Lord uses it and kept when he does not.

And Paul’s argument in the vision reminds us of the most spiritual disguise of “self”: using “I am most useful” to resist being sent. What letting Jesus be King looks like here is: when the Lord says “go,” even if I think staying would be more useful, to rise and go. The focus is not on my usefulness but on his sending.
a: Hear guidance in prayer
The Lord’s guidance mostly comes to those who pray; be quiet first, then plan.
Lay down “I’m most useful”
The Lord’s sending does not depend on where I think I fit; when he says go, I go.
Examine my detonation point
When God blesses someone I think unworthy, is there a voice within me saying “Away with him”?
Identity as a tool
The position and resources God gave me, use when they should be used, for the Lord’s work and not for revenge.
Stand firm in the inborn identity
My place in God’s household was gained by new birth; I need not prove myself every time.
q: Think honestly: recently, has there been someone God blessed while something in you did not quite accept it? What did that touch in you?

Is there an identity, resource or ability that you have been clutching in your own hand to protect yourself? If you placed it in the Lord’s hands, “used when it should be used, kept when it should not,” what would be different today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that more than twenty years ago you told Paul, “They won’t receive your testimony,” and had already prepared the road to the Gentiles for him. Your plan is not built on who is most useful, but only on whom you want to send.
Lord, we admit that within us too is the pride of that crowd—when you bless those we look down on, a voice of “Away with him” has also been in our hearts; and we too often use “I would be most useful staying” to resist your sending. Search our detonation point, remove our VIP-lounge attitude toward grace, and make us remember that we too are unworthy. Teach us, like Paul, to place identity and resources in your hands, to endure when we should endure and speak when we should speak, all for your testimony; and make us stand firm in the identity we were born into in your household, no longer exchanging performance for the place you have freely given. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: But on the next day, desiring to know the truth about why he was accused by the Jews, he freed him from the bonds, and commanded the chief priests and all the council to come together, and brought Paul down and set him before them.
Paul, looking steadfastly at the council, said, “Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today.”
The high priest, Ananias, commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?”
Those who stood by said, “Do you malign God’s high priest?”
Paul said, “I didn’t know, brothers, that he was high priest. For it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’ ”

But when Paul perceived that the one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged!”
When he had said this, an argument arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the crowd was divided.
For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess all of these.

A great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ part stood up, and contended, saying, “We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or angel has spoken to him, let’s not fight against God!”

When a great argument arose, the commanding officer, fearing that Paul would be torn in pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him by force from among them, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night, the Lord stood by him and said, “Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.”
b: In the last devotion, the whip stopped at the last moment; the officer, learning he had bound a Roman citizen, was afraid. But he still did not understand what this man had done to make the whole city want to kill him.

In this devotion, the officer brings Paul before the highest Jewish court—the Sanhedrin—wanting to get to the bottom of it. The result is another confusion. And the end of this passage is the gentlest verse in the whole Jerusalem storm: that night, the Lord stood by Paul.
I. “I have lived before God in all good conscience”—One Sentence, One Slap

In 22:30 to 23:1, the officer released Paul, called together the chief priests and the whole council, and had Paul stand before them. The Sanhedrin was the highest council of the Jews, seventy-one men presided over by the high priest—more than twenty years earlier this same council had tried the Lord Jesus, tried Peter and John, tried Stephen. Paul himself had once carried this council’s letters to arrest people; today he stood in the accused’s place.

“Paul, looking steadfastly at the council”—he did not lower his head. His first sentence was: “Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until this day.” “Lived” in the original means “conducted my life as a citizen,” and “conscience” is a word he often uses in his letters. He was not saying he had no sin, but that from persecuting the church to this day, every step he took was an honest walk according to the God he knew.
• Dare to look steadily: one who is at ease before God need not lower his head before men.
• Conscience must be before God: acting by conscience is not acting by what I feel is right but living before God by his standard.
II. “You whitewashed wall” and “I didn’t know he was the high priest”—What to Do When You Speak Wrongly

In verses 2–5, the high priest Ananias ordered those standing by to strike Paul on the mouth. This Ananias was notorious in history for greed and cruelty; he is recorded as seizing the tithes of the lower priests, and was later killed by his own people during the Jewish revolt.

Paul immediately replied: “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!” “Whitewashed wall” is from Ezekiel (Ezek. 13:10–15): a wall about to fall, with a coat of whitewash on the outside. You sit to judge me according to the law, and yet you command me to be struck contrary to the law. The words were heavy, and also accurate.

Those standing by said, “Do you malign God’s high priest?” Paul at once drew back: “I didn’t know, brothers, that he was high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people’” (Exod. 22:28). Why didn’t he know? Some say his eyesight was poor, some that at this hastily convened meeting the high priest was not in his robes, and some that it was irony—how could such a man be like a high priest.

Whichever it was, the key is his reaction: once it was pointed out that he had gone against Scripture, he immediately returned to Scripture’s position and made no excuses for himself. The man he cursed truly deserved it, but Scripture says do not speak evil of a ruler, so he took it back. Scripture is my standard—and here is what it looks like most concretely: even when I am right, I follow Scripture; even when I have reason, if Scripture says no, I withdraw.
• A word spoken can be taken back: after saying something wrong, the fastest road is to return to Scripture, not to defend myself.
• The standard is higher than emotion: even if the other person is simply wrong, I still treat him according to what is written.
III. “Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged”—Putting the Real Issue on the Table

In verses 6–9, Paul saw that one part of the council were Sadducees and the other Pharisees. The Sadducees were priestly aristocrats who accepted only the Five Books of Moses and did not believe in resurrection, angels or spirits; the Pharisees believed in all of them. Paul cried out: “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged.”

Some say this was Paul’s strategy, deliberately stirring up infighting. But think: which of his words was false? He really was of Pharisaic origin; he really was arrested for preaching Jesus’ resurrection; and resurrection is the heart of the whole gospel. Later before Felix, Festus and Agrippa he spoke of the same thing (24:21, 26:8). He was not changing the subject but putting the real issue on the table: in trying me, you are really trying “whether the dead can rise.”

The result was that the council split, and the scribes of the Pharisees’ party even spoke for him: “We find no evil in this man.” A group who wanted to condemn him began quarreling among themselves first.
• Grasp the core: in debate, don’t sink into side issues; say the one most important thing.
• Resurrection is the foundation: what I believe in is not a system of morality but a Lord who died and lives again.
IV. “Lest Paul should be torn in pieces by them”—Rescued by the Romans a Third Time

In verse 10, “a great dissension arose,” and the officer, “fearing lest Paul should be torn in pieces by them”—“torn in pieces” in the original is “ripped to shreds.” He ordered the soldiers to go down and “take him by force from among them.”

This was the third time in a few days that the Romans rescued Paul: once in the temple, once on the steps, once in the council. The highest Jewish court, which should have been the most reasonable place, was more out of control than the mob in the street; it was instead a Gentile officer who snatched him out again and again. God’s protection came, time after time, wearing a Roman uniform.
• Do not define who the helpers are: God can use unbelievers to protect his servant; do not underestimate any pair of hands in his hand.
V. “The following night, the Lord stood by him”—The Gentlest Verse
In verse 11, “The following night, the Lord stood by him, and said, ‘Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.’”

Think about that night. Paul had been struck on the mouth, shouted at by his brothers to be removed, pulled in two directions, and locked back in the barracks. The Jerusalem he loved did not want him, and obeying the elders and entering the temple had brought all this. If there was ever a night when he might doubt he had taken a wrong turn, it was this night.

On that very night, the Lord came. Not by sending an angel, but the Lord himself “stood by” him. This was the third time in Acts the Lord personally appeared to Paul (18:9, 23:11, 27:23), each at his lowest. Like a hospital ward in the dead of night where a patient wakes and finds someone has been sitting by the bed and has not left—nothing needs to be said; that the person is there is enough.

The Lord said two things. First, “Cheer up”—in the original “take courage,” the very word the Lord used to the disciples on the sea, “Cheer up! It is I” (Matt. 14:27). Second, the Lord gave a verdict on these days in Jerusalem: “as you have testified about me at Jerusalem.” Human eyes saw a failure—beaten, shouted at to be removed, locked up; the Lord saw a testimony. And, “so you must testify also at Rome”—Rome, the place Paul had in his heart to go (19:21), the Lord himself promised. How he would get there the Lord did not say; the coming chapters will tell us he went under escort.
• On the lowest night the Lord comes: not sending someone, but standing by himself.
• The Lord’s verdict differs from men’s: what I think is a failure the Lord calls a testimony.
321 Principles Insight: Scripture Is My Standard, the Lord Is My Presence

In this passage Paul has an imperfect moment: he cursed the high priest. Luke does not cover for him. But from that moment we see something more precious—how he treated his own mistake. He did not say, “He struck me first,” did not say, “What I said was true”; he said: it is written. Scripture is my standard—not only when I am right, but when I have the reason, the other has none, and Scripture says no, it is still the standard. This is what letting Jesus be King looks like in speech: the word was spoken, Scripture stopped it, and I take it back.

And that night the Lord stood by him and gave a verdict on these days in Jerusalem: that was testimony. The self-centered evaluate themselves by results—beaten, driven out, no one believed, so I failed. The self-denying hand the evaluation to the Lord—if he says it is testimony, then it is testimony. The focus on Jesus, not on myself, not on circumstances. When we no longer judge our day by our own eyes, we will find that the Lord has long been standing beside us.
a: Look steadily before God
With a clear conscience before God, I need not lower my head before men.
Return to Scripture when I speak wrongly
Make no excuses; as Scripture says, so I take it back.
Grasp the core
In argument, don’t sink into side issues; say the one most important thing.
Recognize protection in uniform
God can use any pair of hands to shield his servant, unbelievers included.
Hand the verdict to the Lord
The day I think a failure, the Lord may call a testimony.
q: Think of the last time you were “in the right” in a dispute: did you argue your reasons to the end, or were you stopped by a sentence of Scripture? If the latter, did you take it back?

Have you had a stretch of days that you felt were a complete failure—misunderstood, fruitless, wanting to leave? Try handing it to the Lord and letting him say what that stretch was. What would he call it?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that on Paul’s lowest night you stood by him yourself and said, “Cheer up.” Thank you for giving a verdict on those days—not failure but testimony; and thank you for promising Rome, though the way of going was not what he thought.
Lord, we admit that we often forget Scripture when we are in the right, answer back first when struck, and at the end of the day judge our failures with our own eyes. Make your word our real standard, so that even when we are right and the other is wrong we are willing to take back our words according to what is written. On our lowest night, let us recognize that you are standing beside us; and take back our evaluations, letting you say what that day was. May we, as we have testified for you in Jerusalem, testify in the same way in any place you ask us to go. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When it was day, some of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty people who had made this conspiracy.
They came to the chief priests and the elders, and said, “We have bound ourselves under a great curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

Now therefore, you with the council inform the commanding officer that he should bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you were going to judge his case more exactly. We are ready to kill him before he comes near.”
But Paul’s sister’s son heard they were lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul.
Paul summoned one of the centurions, and said, “Bring this young man to the commanding officer, for he has something to tell him.”
So he took him, and brought him to the commanding officer, and said, “Paul, the prisoner, summoned me and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.”
The commanding officer took him by the hand, and going aside, asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though intending to inquire somewhat more accurately concerning him.

Therefore don’t yield to them, for more than forty men lie in wait for him, who have bound themselves under a curse to neither eat nor drink until they have killed him. Now they are ready, looking for the promise from you.”
So the commanding officer let the young man go, charging him, “Tell no one that you have revealed these things to me.”
b: In the last devotion, the Lord stood by Paul in the night and said, “Cheer up! As you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.”

Day broke. The Lord’s promise was still in his ears, and the plot to kill him had already been fixed in the city. More than forty men swore to kill him, the chief priests and elders nodded in cooperation, the plan was thorough, and only the commanding officer’s consent was awaited. And the one who dismantled the whole scheme was a young man whose name is not even given in Scripture. This devotion shows us how bad religious zeal can become, and how ordinary God’s protection can be.
I. “Neither to eat nor drink until they had killed Paul”—Zeal, but Without God

In verses 12–15, “When it was day”—the Lord’s promise came “the following night,” the plot “when it was day.” More than forty men “conspired and bound themselves with an oath”—in the original, “placed themselves under a curse”: if we fail, may God curse us. They treated murder as a vow to God, and fasting as preparation before killing.

Even more terrible are verses 14 and 15: they went to the chief priests and elders, and these spiritual leaders did not stop them but cooperated—“as though you were going to judge his case more exactly,” using a false hearing to lure Paul halfway and kill him. Religion became a cover for murder.

Did these men have zeal? Yes, so hot they would neither eat nor drink. But a sentence Paul later wrote was written exactly for them: “they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2). Paul himself had once been such a man—“still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” (9:1), taking the council’s letters to arrest people. He knew very well what such zeal was: “self” dressed in religious clothes. When I am convinced I am working for God, I feel any means is permissible, because the goal is God’s.
• Zeal is not credentials: fasting from food and drink can also be fasting for my own hatred; zeal counts only if it follows Scripture.
• Beware of “for God” means: once I feel I can do anything for God, that “God” is usually myself.
II. “Paul’s sister’s son heard”—God’s Protection in the Plainest Clothes
In verse 16, “But Paul’s sister’s son heard of their lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul.”

This is the only time Scripture mentions Paul’s relatives. He had a sister living in Jerusalem, and the sister had a son, a “young man,” perhaps only a boy of ten-odd years. How did he hear it? Luke does not say. Perhaps in the market, perhaps at a relative’s house, perhaps those forty men were too pleased with themselves and not careful enough in their talk. In any case, a boy heard.

Last night the Lord himself said “Cheer up” to Paul; today the Lord’s protection came—not an angel, not an earthquake, but a nephew. God’s protection often wears the plainest clothes: a sentence a child overheard, a friend’s casual reminder, a small illness that makes you change your plans. We often ask God for miracles, yet he often uses a person.
The oath of forty men, with the support of chief priests and elders, against a nameless young man. To human eyes the odds were lopsided; to God, one obedient person was enough.
• God uses people, not always miracles: today’s protection from God may be the word of the person beside me; don’t miss it.
• Without a name there is still a place: in God’s system there are no small people; one young man can stop forty adults.
III. “Bring this young man to the commanding officer”—With a Promise, Still Use Your Hands

In verses 17–19, when Paul heard, he “called one of the centurions” and asked him to take the young man to the commanding officer. Rome at the time allowed prisoners to receive visits from relatives and friends; though Paul was in custody in the barracks, he could still call on a centurion, which showed the officer already viewed this Roman citizen with some regard.

Notice Paul’s reaction. Last night the Lord himself said he would surely reach Rome—since the Lord had promised, he could have lain down and waited for a miracle. But he did not. He took action at once: found the centurion, sent his nephew, followed procedure. The Lord’s promise did not make him passive; it made him clearer-headed.

This is an important distinction: relying on the Spirit with the heart is not failing to use the hands. Faith is not putting hands in pockets waiting for God to act; faith is knowing God will accomplish it, so I use every pair of hands and every road he gives me to cooperate with his accomplishing. The promise is God’s; the action is mine. There is no contradiction here, only cooperation.

The officer “took him by the hand, and going aside, asked him privately”—an officer commanding a thousand men, taking a boy’s hand. The picture is beautiful. God prepared not only a boy to bring the news, but also an officer willing to listen to a boy.
• A promise is not lying down to wait: when the Lord says it will be done, I should all the more do well the step I am to take.
• Willing to listen to the small: the officer took the boy’s hand; God often puts the most important words in the mouths of the smallest.
IV. “Don’t yield to them”—A Young Man’s Courage and Clarity

In verses 20–22, the young man told the whole plot: the Jews had agreed that tomorrow they would ask you to bring Paul down to the council, pretending to inquire more closely; more than forty were lying in wait, had sworn an oath, and were ready, “only waiting for the promise from you.” Then he said something a grown man would say: “Therefore don’t yield to them.”

This boy had courage and also order. He knew whom he was speaking to, and knew the person across from him might be the one being used. He did not add embellishment, only explained clearly, and then warned: don’t yield to them.
The officer believed him, sent him away, and charged him not to tell anyone—he would handle it quietly, which is the content of the next devotion.

A tiny fuse, when the whole circuit is about to catch fire, blows, and the whole house is saved. It is small, unnoticeable, and burned out no one remembers its name. But without it, the fire would have entered the house. This young man was that fuse. What he did required no learning, no eloquence, only to say what he knew at the time it should be said.
• Speak clearly, without embellishment: telling plainly what I know is itself a service.
• Speak when it should be spoken: if the young man had stayed silent because he was small and feared trouble, the oath of the forty would have succeeded.
321 Principles Insight: There Are No Small People in God’s System

In this passage there are two kinds of “one mind.” More than forty men swore “with one mind,” and the chief priests and elders cooperated with one mind—this is the one mind of self: a group’s “selves” gathered together using God’s name to do what they wanted. On the other side, a young man, a centurion, an officer, and a prisoner, four people each taking a step of their own, no one grabbing credit, no one gaining fame, yet they dismantled the whole plot. This is what God’s system in operation looks like: not an organizational structure, but a group of people obeying in their own places.

Building God’s system is not building a large organization but accompanying each person to become an overcomer in his own place. The young man’s place was to hear and go and tell; Paul’s place was not to lie down and wait but to use his hands to cooperate with the promise; the officer’s place was to take a child’s hand and listen. Each person returning to his place, letting God be God and man be man—this is humility, and it is also why the plot failed.

And last night’s promise and today’s action give us a clear lesson: the Spirit’s guidance and human action never conflict. The Lord said he would surely reach Rome, and Paul called the centurion. Rely on the Spirit with the heart, then do well what is in your hands.
a: Check my zeal
Can the methods I use in doing things for God stand the test of Scripture?
Recognize ordinary protection
The reminder from the person beside me today may be the nephew God sent.
With a promise, still use hands
When the Lord says it will be done, I should all the more do well the step I am to take.
Be willing to listen to the smallest
Like the officer taking the boy’s hand, take the words of the smallest seriously.
Speak when it is time to speak
Say clearly what I know, without embellishment, and without closing my mouth for fear of trouble.
q: Was there a time when, for the sake of “God’s work,” you used methods not in line with Scripture—saying something untrue, hurting someone, taking a shortcut? In that zeal, whom were you actually serving?
Looking back over the past year, has God used a very ordinary person or a very ordinary sentence to protect you? Did you recognize it then? What can you do for that person today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that on the morning when forty men swore their oath you had already arranged a young man who would hear. Thank you for letting us see that your protection often wears the plainest clothes and that there are no small people in your system.
Lord, we admit that within us too is that zeal dressed in religious clothes, feeling anything is allowed for your sake; we also often ask for miracles and miss the people you send; we hold your promises while keeping our hands in our pockets, waiting. Cleanse our zeal so that it follows your word; open our eyes to recognize the one beside us who brings the news; and make us, after receiving a promise, all the more clear-headed to do well the step we are to take. May each of us return to our own place—the one who hears go and tell, the one in authority willing to listen, the one imprisoned still using his hands—so that your plan may be accomplished among us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: He called to himself two of the centurions, and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen, and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night.”
He asked them to provide animals, that they might set Paul on one, and bring him safely to Felix the governor.
He wrote a letter like this:
“Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings.
“This man was seized by the Jews, and was about to be killed by them, when I came with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman.
Desiring to know the cause why they accused him, I brought him down to their council.
I found him to be accused about questions of their law, but not to be charged with anything worthy of death or of imprisonment.
When I was told that the Jews lay in wait for the man, I sent him to you immediately, charging his accusers also to bring their accusations against him before you. Farewell.”
So the soldiers, carrying out their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
But on the next day they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the barracks.
When they came to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.
When the governor had read it, he asked what province he was from. When he understood that he was from Cilicia, he said,
“I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.” He commanded that he be kept in Herod’s palace.
b: In the last devotion, a young man reported the ambush of more than forty men to the commanding officer, and the officer charged him not to tell anyone, to handle it quietly.

This devotion is how he handled it. That night, four hundred seventy Roman soldiers escorted one prisoner out of the city. From a human viewpoint it was an urgent military transfer; from God’s viewpoint it was the first step of the Lord’s promise of the night before—the road to Rome began that night.
I. “Two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, two hundred men armed with spears”—Four Hundred Seventy Soldiers Escorting One Man

In verses 23 and 24, the officer called two centurions and ordered: two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen, to be ready “from the third hour of the night”—nine o’clock in the evening—to go to Caesarea. Mounts were also to be provided for Paul to ride, and he was to be brought safely to Felix the governor.

Four hundred seventy soldiers. The garrison in the barracks was about a thousand; he committed nearly half to escort one man. Because he knew that more than forty men lay in ambush in the city, and if word leaked, the road could turn into an ambush; and since Paul was a Roman citizen, he had already broken the law once by binding him and dared not risk it again.

But we must see another layer: the Lord who said “Cheer up” to Paul the night before used the army of the Roman Empire tonight to keep his word. No one would send out four hundred seventy soldiers for a poor preacher; but that King would. When God’s will moves forward, even an unbelieving empire opens the road and prepares the horses.

It is like an armored cash truck. When you see one on the street with armed guards front and back, it is not because the truck itself is valuable but because of what is inside. That night Rome was escorting a prisoner it thought of no importance, while heaven was escorting a witness who would carry the gospel to Rome.
• The Lord’s promise has feet: what he said last night, tonight began to walk with four hundred seventy soldiers.
• Do not think lightly of the worth of being escorted: in the Lord’s eyes, a person who testifies for him is worth an entire empire’s troop movement.
II. “Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix, greetings”—A Slightly Polished Official Letter

In verses 25–27, the officer wrote an official letter. It is one of the few official documents preserved in full in the New Testament, in standard form: writer, recipient, greeting. At last we know his name: Claudius Lysias.

The recipient Felix had been an imperial slave who, after being freed, rose through his brother’s connections at court to become governor of Judea. The historian’s verdict on him was: “He exercised the power of a king with the spirit of a slave.” Such a man was about to decide Paul’s fate.

Now look at verse 27, how Lysias described himself: “Having learned that he was a Roman, I came with the soldiers and rescued him.” What was the fact? When he went down with soldiers he had no idea who Paul was, and bound him with two chains, and only when the whip was about to fall did he learn he was a Roman. But in the letter this became “having learned he was a Roman, I rescued him”—writing himself as a far-sighted hero and wiping out the nearly illegal act entirely.

This is too much like us. When writing a report or telling a story, we pass lightly over our own mistakes and move the credit forward a little—not lying, just polishing. What “self” is best at is not lying but editing. And Luke places the letter and the facts side by side so that we can see the traces of the editing for ourselves.
• Tell about myself honestly: when I tell a story, have I cut out my own mistakes and moved the credit forward?
• Letting Jesus receive glory begins with not editing: one who gives glory to the Lord does not need to be the hero of his own version.
III. “Nothing worthy of death or of imprisonment”—Rome Declares Him Innocent the First Time

In verses 28–30, Lysias went on to say that he brought Paul down to the council to find out, “and found him to be accused about questions of their law, but not to be charged with anything worthy of death or of imprisonment.” Then he told of the ambush, sent Paul on, and ordered his accusers to bring their case before the governor.

“Nothing worthy of death or of imprisonment”—this is the first official Roman declaration of Paul’s innocence. More will follow: Festus said he “had committed nothing worthy of death” (25:25), and Agrippa said, “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar” (26:32). Time after time, Gentile officials could find no crime.

This reminds us of another. Pilate also said three times: “I find no basis for a charge against this man” (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). The Lord Jesus was condemned though innocent, Paul imprisoned though innocent—the two roads are one. The gospel has never been persecuted because it broke the law, but because it proclaims that the dead are raised and that Jesus is Lord, for which no crime can be found in human law, yet which human pride cannot tolerate.
• Innocent, yet in chains: those who follow the Lord may be completely blameless and still not free; this is not failure.
• Walk the road the Lord walked: no crime could be found in him, and none in me; he was still handed over, and I may be too.
IV. “By night to Antipatris” “When your accusers come”—The Road to Rome Begins with Being Escorted

In verses 31–35, the soldiers, “as it was commanded them,” brought Paul by night to Antipatris—a city built by Herod the Great in memory of his father Antipater, about sixty kilometers from Jerusalem, a night’s forced march. Out of the hill country of Judea, the danger of ambush had passed; the next day the infantry returned to the barracks, and the seventy horsemen continued escorting him to Caesarea.

Caesarea—a few days earlier Paul had gone up to Jerusalem from here, Agabus had bound his own hands and feet with a belt here, and everyone here had urged him not to go. Now he returned, bound, under the escort of Gentiles, just as foretold. But look: “handed over to the Gentiles,” and the result was that the Gentiles’ hands saved his life. The way God’s prophecies are fulfilled is often much gentler than we fear.

Felix read the letter and asked what province he was from—Cilicia belonged to the province of Syria, and Felix had authority to try the case. He said, “I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive,” and commanded that Paul be kept in “Herod’s palace”—the royal palace built by Herod the Great, now the governor’s residence. Paul’s stay there would be two years (24:27).

Two years. The Lord had promised Rome, but next came two years of waiting at Caesarea. The promise was not broken, only the road was longer than thought. The self-denying have a visible look here: he does not hurry God. Rome is the Lord’s promise; when and how to get there is the Lord’s business; how to live each day at Caesarea is mine.
• Fulfillment gentler than fear: the binding God spoke of really came, yet within the way it came was his protection.
• Do not hurry God: the place the Lord promised will come, and the waiting in between is also his road, not delay.
321 Principles Insight: Let Jesus Be King, and Even an Empire Moves Troops for Him

From chapter 21 to here, Paul arranged nothing himself. He was seized, bound, carried, snatched out, escorted—in every verb he was the object. Yet looking back, all this was carrying him toward Rome. The Lord said last night, “so you must testify also at Rome,” and tonight the army of Rome prepared horses for him.

This is the truth of letting Jesus be King: not that I arrange everything, but that he arranges everything and I need only be faithful at each moment. The self-centered cannot bear being the object—being arranged, escorted, made to wait two years makes them feel out of control. The self-denying know that the subject is that King, and being the object is just right. Self-denial is not nothing but entering the limitless—Paul alone could not have walked to Rome, but four hundred seventy soldiers, a letter, and a governor, all arranged by the Lord, carried him there.

And Lysias’s slightly polished letter reminds us where the glory goes. Letting Jesus receive all the glory, the most everyday exercise is not editing when I tell about myself—mistakes stay, credit is not moved, because the true subject is not me.
a: Believe the promise has feet
What the Lord says, he himself will move everything to accomplish, including unbelievers and institutions.
Don’t edit myself
When telling a story, leave the mistakes in, don’t move the credit, and leave the hero’s place to the Lord.
Be willing to be bound though innocent
Being blameless yet not free is not failure; it is the road the Lord walked.
Recognize gentle fulfillment
The difficulty God spoke of will come, but within the way it comes is his protection.
Don’t hurry God
The promised place will come, and the two years between are also his road; live each day well.
q: Recall the last time you told about something you did: was any part “edited”—mistakes passed over lightly, credit moved forward a little? What would it look like to retell it according to the facts?
Are you now in a “Caesarea”—the Lord’s promise not yet arrived, and the road longer than you thought? Are you hurrying God, or living each day of the waiting well?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that on the night Paul was escorted you kept your word of the night before with four hundred seventy Roman soldiers. Thank you for letting us see that your promise has feet, that even an empire that does not know you prepares horses and opens the road for your servant, and that the way you fulfill prophecy is far gentler than we fear.
Lord, we admit that we cannot bear to be the object—arranged, made to wait, brought to places we did not choose; and we often edit when we tell about ourselves. Make us willing to let you be the subject, faithful at each moment, handing over where we go and when we arrive into your hands. Remove from us the self that wants to be the hero, and make us honest when we tell our stories, so that all the glory goes to you. If you want us to wait two years at Caesarea, give us a calm that does not hurry you, for we know the Rome you spoke of will surely come. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: After five days, the high priest, Ananias, came down with certain elders and an orator, one Tertullus. They informed the governor against Paul.
When he was called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, “Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace, and that prosperity is coming to this nation by your foresight,
we accept it in all ways and in all places, most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness.
But that I don’t delay you, I entreat you to bear with us and hear a few words.
For we have found this man to be a plague, an instigator of insurrections among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He even tried to profane the temple, and we arrested him.
By examining him yourself you may ascertain all these things of which we accuse him.”
The Jews also joined in the attack, affirming that these things were so.
b: In the last devotion, more than forty Jews swore neither to eat nor drink until they had killed Paul, and the commanding officer Lysias mobilized four hundred seventy soldiers overnight to escort Paul out of Jerusalem all the way to Caesarea. Governor Felix read the letter, said, “I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive,” and had Paul kept in Herod’s palace.

Leaving under the escort of more than four hundred soldiers looked like an escape; but at Caesarea what awaited him was not freedom but another trial. The accusers arrived, and brought a professional lawyer.
I. “After five days… a certain orator, Tertullus”—The Other Side Came Prepared
In verse 1, “After five days, the high priest Ananias came down with certain elders and an orator, one Tertullus. They informed the governor against Paul.”

“Five days” was quick. From Jerusalem to Caesarea is about a hundred kilometers; to gather the elders, hire a lawyer, prepare the papers and make the whole trip in five days was already hurrying. The assassination in the previous chapter had failed, so this chapter turned to the legal route—the method changed, the goal did not.

“Orator” in the original is “rhetorician,” a professional courtroom advocate. Tertullus is a Latin name, and he probably knew Roman legal procedure. The high priest Ananias came in person—the very high priest of chapter 23 who ordered Paul struck on the mouth—showing that in their eyes this was a case they must win.
• Recognize the pattern of attack: Satan never attacks carelessly; if assassination fails, he goes to court, and always returns in a different form.
• No need to prepare for battle yourself: Paul had no lawyer and no five days of preparation; he had only the Lord’s “Cheer up” of the night before (23:11).
II. “Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace”—Lies Told Beautifully

In verses 2–4, as soon as Tertullus opened his mouth, there was first a long stretch of flattery: “Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace, and that worthy deeds are done for this nation by your foresight, we accept it always and in all places, most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness.”

This was the standard opening in the courts of the day, called “winning favor.” But what these words said would make anyone who knew a little history blush. Felix had come from slavery, and Roman historians described him as “exercising a king’s power with a slave’s spirit”; riots rose one after another during his term, and he ruled by harshness and bloodshed, not “foresight.” The Jews hated him to the bone, yet now their lawyer said “with all thankfulness.”

The most powerful thing about a lie is not that it is crude but that it is beautiful. Every sentence of Tertullus was fitting, and not one was sincere. If a person’s mouth has learned to say “with all thankfulness” when needed, his heart has already left its place. When people need something from someone, they become especially good at reading faces; this cleverness is not given by the Holy Spirit.
• Examine my mouth: of what I say to superiors, elders, those in power, how much is sincere and how much is “winning favor”?
• The truth needs no packaging: Paul’s opening in the next devotion is only one true sentence—“Because I know that you have been for many years a judge to this nation, I cheerfully make my defense.”
III. “A plague”—Three Charges, Each Heavier Than the Last
Verses 5 and 6 are the body of the accusation, three charges in all.

First, “stirs up insurrections among all the Jews throughout the world.” This was a political crime. “Insurrections” in the original means “sedition, agitation,” the offense the Roman Empire could least tolerate, punishable by death. Tertullus deliberately said “throughout the world” so that Felix would handle Paul from Rome’s standpoint.

Second, “a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.” “Sect” in the original means “faction,” not itself a bad word; but with “Nazarenes” attached, it carries contempt—a group started by a carpenter from a small town in Galilee, with Paul as ringleader.

Third, “who tried to profane the temple.” This was a religious crime, and the only one for which Rome allowed the Jews to carry out the death penalty themselves. In chapter 21 the Jews from Asia “supposed” Paul had brought Gentiles into the temple; now in court “supposed” had become “tried”—they themselves knew the evidence was insufficient.

And before the three charges, Tertullus first gave Paul a title: “a plague.” Once a person is given such a label, whatever he says will be treated as the spread of a virus. We often do the same to people—“he’s that kind of person”—and afterward whatever he does is read through that label. A label is the easiest judgment and the most unjust.
• Don’t casually apply labels: before passing judgment on someone, ask: am I seeing facts, or a conclusion already decided?
• Don’t fear labels: Paul was called a plague and did not lose his identity; who I am is not decided by those who accuse me.
IV. “We arrested him”—Calling Our Own Violence Law Enforcement

From the second half of verse 6 to verse 8, Tertullus said: “We arrested him.” Some ancient manuscripts continue: we wanted to judge him according to our law, but the commanding officer Lysias “came and with great violence took him away.”
